summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 on the net wealth of the assessee. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,00,000 as the net wealth. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that accrued interest was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessments. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner followed the decision of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Vedrevu Venkappa Rao vs Commissioner of Wealth Tax, West Bengal, (A.I.R. 1965 Andhra Pradesh. The High Court held that the assessee was liable to pay interest on accrual basis. The High court held that the income tax Officer was in law justified in including in the net wealth the net wealth and debts of the assessee on the outstandings of the money lending business. The High. Court also held that the interest was liable for inclusion in the net assets of the assessee 's business. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the assessee had not been assessed to wealth Tax for the assessment year 1965 66, and that the income Tax Officer included in the net income of the assessee interest due on accrual basis, though not realised, on the out standings of the amount lending business, was liable to tax. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The computation of the net wealth by the Wealth Tax Officer is correct. The computation is correct. [309F] 2. The computation has to be made on the basis of the last day of the year. [309G] 3. The computation should be made on a particular date. [309A] 4. The computation must be made on that date. [310C] 5. The computation in terms of the last date of the income tax "previous year" is not permissible. [309D] 6. The computation made by the Wealth tax Officer is correct and the computation made by him is correct. It is apparent that what accrues as a right also falls to be included within the assets of an assessee under the Wealth Tax Act. That being so, the conclusion is inescapable that even though the accounts of the assessee are maintained on cash basis interest due on accrued basis, thoughnot realised, on outstandings, on the Outstandings of money lending business are liable to be excluded in the net Wealth of the assessee.[309F] 7. The computation under section 7 is correct and does not require any consideration of the assessee employing one system of accounting or another. [309H] 8. The computation cannot be made on any other basis. [309B] 9. The computation can be made on an objective basis.

The respondent was dismissed from service on the ground of defi cation of certain charges. The respondent challenged the order of dismissal by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court set aside the order of the Tribunal and directed the Governor to review the penalty. The High court held that the respondent was not a workman and the Tribunal could not have interfered with the penalty if the conclusion of the Inquiry Officer was based on evidence even if some of it was found to be irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. The High Cour t dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent had not been given any opportunity to defend the charge and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the penalty. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have the jurisdiction to interfere in the matter of punishment if the conclusion arrived at by the Inquiry Officer or the Tribunal prima facie make out a case of misdemeanour for which the punishment can lawfully be imposed. [27F] 2. The HighCourt has no jurisdiction if the findings of the Inquiry officer or the Tribunal are based on evidence, even if some are found to be relevant or extraneous to it. The High Cou rt has no jurisdiction to entertain a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. [27H] 3. The High courts have the jurisdiction under Article 226 to interfere with an order of punishment if it is found that the conclusion of disciplinary authority or the Tribunal is based on evidence. [27A] 4. The High ourt has no jurisdiction in a writ petition over a decision of the Tribunal. The High cour t has no jurisdiction. [27D] 5. The High turt has no power to interfere with a penalty if the finding of the Inquiry Office or the Tribunal was based on any evidence even if any of it is found to be extraneous or extraneous to or extraneous to, the matter. [27E] 6. The High Turt has no juris diction to direct the Governor to reconsider the penalty, for as long as the finding of misconduct is based on the evidence even if certain of it is not found to be germane or extraneous to that matter. [28F] 7.

The appellants were the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff in a suit filed by the respondent No.1 for a declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao '. The suit was decreed by the trial Court. The first appellate court dismissed the suit holding that the suit was barred by the principle of res judicata in view of the dismissal of the former suit No. 157 of 1968. The second appeal was dismissed by the High Court. In the second appeal before this Court, the appellants contended that the suit being barred by the principles of res judicata, the subsequent suit was barred under the principle of Res judicata. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The jurisdiction of the civil court is specifically barred by section 58(2) of the Act. The jurisdiction is vested in the Mamlatdar under section 7 of the Act and section 58(1) specifically bars the jurisdiction of all other courts to settle, decide or deal with any question which is by or under the Act required to be settled, decided or dealt with by the Mamlatdar. [32F G] 1.2 The jurisdiction of civil court is expressly barred by section58(2) from settling, deciding or dealing with any question referred to in section 4(2) or section 8(2) in which case, obviously, it could be argued that the second suit based on the factum of tenancy was not maintainable. [32G] 1.3 The jurisdiction is conferred on the Mamlatdar under Section 7 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The jurisdiction of Civil Court is specifically barred under section 58(3) of the Bombay Act. [32H] 1.4 The jurisdiction is, therefore, vested in the Civil Court. [32A] 1.5 The jurisdiction is not conferred on the Civil Court by section 58 (2) of Act. The Civil Court would not be competent to pass any order for restoration of possession to the deemed tenant. [32B] 1.6 The jurisdiction is to be exercised by the Mamlatdar under the Bombay Tenancy Act. [33C] 1.7 The jurisdiction is a vested in the civil court. The jurisdiction under section 58 (3) is specifically barred. [33D] 1.8 The jurisdiction is an inherent power of the Mamlatdar under sections 7 and 58 (2). [33D E] 1.9 The jurisdiction is inherent in the Mamlatdar. The jurisdiction has to be exercised in accordance with the provisions of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879. [33E] 1.10 The jurisdiction is discretionary. The jurisdiction can be exercised by a civil court only if the Mamlatdar has decided the question of tenancy. If on the other hand he is held to be tenant, the Civil Court may consider passing of a decree in eviction but if on the other, he is held not to be tenant the Civil Court can pass any order in eviction. [33F] 1.11 The jurisdiction is also conferred on the civil court to decide whether the suit is barred by the provisions of section 58(4) of the Tenancy Act. The Mamlatdar has to decide the question of status as tenant. If on such a question, the Mamlatdar decides the question of relationship of tenancy, he has to decide or deal With the same. [33G] 1:12. The jurisdiction conferred on the Collector under section 7 is specifically barred in view of section 58 (1) of the Maharashtra Tenancy and Agricultural Land Act, 1948, and section 58 (4) specifically bars jurisdiction of all courts to settle and decide any question which was by or under this Act required to settle, decided or deal with the same.

The petitioners are working as daily rated employees. They are termed as daily rated workers. They are described as daily rated employee. They are called as daily rated workmen. They are being paid the minimum wages admissible to them. The Corporation has not fixed the mini mum wages payable to the petitioners engaged in the Corporation or other similar industries. The Corporation, however, adopted the minimum wages payable to them. They have been treated as construction workers. The Corporation have also fixed the minimum wages applicable to similar work in the construction industry. The petitioners have been treated in the same cadre on the basis of their qualifications, duties and responsibilities of the posts concerned. The petitioners are claiming wages payable to regular employees in Government service. The petitioners claim that they are entitled to the same pay as regular employees. The petitioners also claim payment of the same wages as were paid to the carpenters, painters and carpenters. The petitioners, therefore, seek enforcement of their fundamental right to have "equal pay for equal work" under Article 14 of the Constitution. The petitioners seek enforcement of the right to "equal pay" for equal work. The petitioners pray for enforcement of their right to " equal pay for equal works". The petitioners have filed this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for enforcement of the fundamental right to "equally recruited workers" under Article 16 of the Constitution, contending that the Corporation has reduced its overheads and maintained only the administrative staff in the production centers at different parts of the State and no permanent craftsmen are employed. The petitioners further contended that the Corporation had reduced its overhead and maintained only those employees who execute the work in their own homes. The petitioners therefore, seek to enforce their right to equal pay for Equal work. The respondents have filed counter affidavit. The petitioners contended that the petitioners are not entitled to equal pay. The petitioners submit that the Corporation is not bound to pay the same to the petitioners, that the Corporation should fix the minimum wages for similar work in construction industry. They have also contended that the State Government has not fixed minimum wages for identical work in the Construction industry. The Corporation also contended that it has reduced its own overheads and maintaining only the administrative Staff in the production centres at different parts. The petitioners submitted that the Corporation was not justified in fixing the minimum wages. The petitioners relied on the decision of Randhir Singh case, and contended that the principle of equal pay for similar work cannot be enforced. The petitioners filed rejoinder affidavit. The respondents submitted that the petitioners have been discriminated against in respect of the work done by them. The petitioners were paid the minimum wage admissible to them and the minimum wages were payable to them, and that the Corporation have reduced its overhead. The petitioners prayed for the enforcement of their rights to equal pay and equal work. Allowing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The petitioners cannot enforce the right to equal work. They have not been extended to employees of the Corporation. The petitioners can claim the same pay for equal employment. The petitioners should be paid the minimum pay admissible to such workmen. The petitioners may claim the same scale of pay as were paid by the Corporation. [667C D] 2. The petitioners ' jobs are comparable with the counterparts in the Government service. They are paid the minimum Wages admissible to such employees. The Corporation is not justified in directing the Corporation to apply the rates prescribed under exhibit P.

The prosecution case against the accused 1 to 4 was that on the night of October 1975 at Babultara and Waghala villages, all the seven accused and the approver P.W. 2 were present at the scene of occurrence. The approver P.Ws. 2, 3, 4, 5 and 7 were the close relatives of the deceased and the approver. The approver was the only person to whom the approver was examined. The approver had stated that he had seen the deceased and his wife in the house of the deceased at Babultar and that he had gone to the house of P.W 2 and had seen the accused and the deceased going towards the house of one of the accused. The approver also stated that he was not present at the time of the occurrence. The prosecution case was that the approver P was not present when the approver was called and that he was present at the place of occurrence. On the other hand, the approver P stated that he did not know the accused and that he did so at the time when the approver had gone to his house. The approver further stated that he knew the accused and he had seen him going towards the place of incident. The approver stated that he saw the deceased and P.W 1 going towards the village of the deceased. The approver, however, stated that he could not see the accused and P.Ws 1 and 2. The approver 's evidence was that he had heard the deceased and others going towards the spot and that he saw him going towards his house and that he heard the deceased going out of the house and that the accused had come to the house and asked him to come out of the village. The approver then went to the house where the deceased was found and found the deceased lying dead. The approver gave a statement to the police that he had not seen the accused. He also stated that the approver had not seen him and that he could identify the accused. On the question whether the approver had been rightly convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for life under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. the High Court held that the approver was not a party to the conspiracy and that he has been rightly convicted. The High Court also held that the retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against accused 6 in view of the fact that he was a party to conspiracy and that the approver 's statement was not corroborated by the approver. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the State that the retracted Judicial confession of accused 1 and 6 could not be used against them in view of section 114 of the Evidence Act and that the retracted confession of accused 2 could not be acted upon. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confession is not a substantive piece of evidence and it is not a piece of evidence. It is a substantive piece and is not a part of the evidence. It can be used only for the purpose of corroboration of the evidence of the approver. [604D] 2. The retracted Judicial confession is not substantive evidence and it can be used for corroboration of the testimony of the approver in the case of other evidence. [605E] 3. The retracted confession of the accused can be used against him in the case where the evidence is of a circumstantial nature and it is a weak piece of evidence which can be used to corroborate the testimony of a witness. [606F] 4. The retracted evidence of the accused is not a weak piece and is a weak evidence. It cannot be used against the accused in view of Section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. [607H] 5. The retracted confessional statement of accused 5 can be used as substantive evidence and the retracted confession can be used in support of the conviction of the accused in the case. [608H] 6. The retracted confessions of accused 5 and 6 are not substantive evidence.

The appellant executed a will in favour of his wife, his father, his brother and his brother. The will was executed by the testator in the presence of the testator and the testator. The testator was in a sound and disposing state of mind or that it represented her intentions. The testator had signed the will in the presence and the testator signed the will. The testator died in the year 1945. The testator, his wife, executed a will on August 22, 1945, in favour of the appellant. The testator 's death was not in dispute. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the will was not true and that the testator had executed the will in his presence and that the will had been executed by his wife in the presence, of the testator. He also claimed that the testator was in sound and disposing of state of mind and that the execution of the will was a fraud on the testator. It was contended that the testator 's signature on the will was an admitted one and that the signature of the testator was not proved to be the last will and testament of the testator, and that the High Court was in error in coming to the conclusion that the will in question was not proved. Held, that the High court was in error of law in coming to its conclusion that the testator did not execute the will in respect of any of the properties mentioned in the will. It was not necessary to examine the evidence of the testator to prove the execution of a will. The will in question did not contain the signature of any testator. The will did not contain any signature of the deceased. The testator did not at all support the appellant 's case about previous instruction. The will had not been proved to be a will executed by the deceased. It was a will executed in the presence or disposing state of the mind of the testator that he understood the nature and effect of the dispositions before he put his signature to the will.

The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of Arcotors, a motor carbons, manufactured by it. The appellant company was registered as a dealer under the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The appellant was registered as dealer under the Act. The appellant filed returns for the assessment years 1965 66 and 1966 77 on the ground that they fell under entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule of the Act. In the returns filed by the appellant the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed the appellant 's appeal and set aside the order of the Sales Tax Tribunal. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to adduce evidence to determine the question whether they fell under Entry No. 4. The High court held that the main use of the arc carbons under consideration was duly proved to be that of production of powerful light used in projectors in cinemas. The High. Court also held that the sales tax authorities were justified in disallowing the claim of the appellant for adducing evidence to determine whether they fell within entry No.4 of the 1 st Schedule of the Andhra Pradesh State General Sales Tax, 1957. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in holding that the main user of the arc Carbons under Item 4 of the First Schedule of the Madras General Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1957 was duly proved and that the appellant had failed to prove that they fell within the relevant entry No. 1 of the First schedule of the Act and that the sales Tax Appellate Tribunal was justified in allowing the appeal. HELD: (1) The word "accessories" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. It will be noticed that the entry in each case. is used in a schedule in which description of goods to be taxed indicate that the expression "required for use" has been employed for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. The first entry in the schedule relates to "motor vehicles" and includes "component parts of motor vehicles". The second entry relates to "component part of motor vehicles" and "articles (including batteries adapted for use as parts and accessories of motor vehicles." but excludes certain other articles by putting in the words "not being such articles as are ordinarily also used for other purposes". [562 E F] (2) The word 'accessories ' is used in two entries, namely, "parts thereof" and "accessories". The word "parts" is used both in the schedule and in the schedule. The word "attached" is used for the purpose of indicating the connection between the motor vehicles to be taxed. [562 G H] (3) The word used in the first entry is "accessories", which are required for use in projectors or other cinematographic equipment. It will therefore be noticed that in the instant case the word "accessory" is used. [562 A] (4) The word in the first and the second entry is used in both the entries, namely "parts of motor vehicles", and "arilators" which are required to be used in projector or other cinemas. [562 C] (5) The word is used in various entries, such as entry No.

The petitioners, who were the owners of a quarry lease, challenged the validity of the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966, by filing writ petitions in the High Court of Gujarat. The High Court dismissed the petitions. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the royalty levied and covered under the Rules should be applied only for mineral development and since the said royalty is being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State, the levy was bad. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The Act is passed for devel opment of minerals, but while discharging its functions relating to development, if the State incidentally allows mining to be carried on in the public interest and levies in that connection a tax, it does not mean that the said tax should be used only for development of minerals and not for other purposes sanctioned by law. Under the Act, the State Government is empowered to make rules for regulating the grant of quarry leases, mining leases or other mineral concessions in re spect of minor minerals and for purposes connected there with. Rule 18 of the Rules provides for the determination of the rate of royalty payable in respect of minor minerals. The State Government is also empowered to make Rules for the determination and collection of royalty. [408C D] 2. The Act does not authorise the State Government to show any concession while promulgating the Rules which are in the nature of subordi nate legislation. [407D] 3. The Act, therefore, is passed for denovo consideration of the State indirectly allowing mining to be done in the public interests and levies in the said connection a tax. [410E] 4. The Act provides for the fixation of the rate or royalty payable in the State of Gujarat on minor minerals. [412F] 5. The Act also provides for the levy of royalty in respect of major minerals. [409F] 6. The Act has been passed for deaf earment of minerals and the area or land covered by a mining lease is governed by rule 15 which says that no quarry lease shall be granted for an area exceeding 10 hectares in case of specified minor mineral and 20 hec tares in the case of other minerals. So a comparison of the relevant rules would show that a larger restriction is imposed both on the area in respect of which a Parwana could be issued and the duration of the Parwana right and as also stated that the persons who take quarrying Parwana are persons belonging to the weaker sections of society and if under rule 21 a concession is shown in their favour it cannot be said that there is no reasonable nexus between the classification for purposes of the proviso to rule 21 to show concession in the matter of payment of royalty and the social policy underlying the Constitution, the statute and the Rules.

The appellant was the trustee of a temple. He took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship of the temple was not hereditary. The High Court held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the succession was not hereditary, that the appellant had no hereditary right to the office of trustee and that the suit was not barred by limitation. HELD: (1) The appellant was a mere hereditary trustee and the suit was barred by limitation, and the High Court was right in setting aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge. [435 B] (2) The word "regulated by usage" in section 6(8) of the Act must be construed along with the phrase "succession to this office" and when so construed that part of the definition would only apply where the ordinary rules of succession under the Hindu law are modified by usage and succession has to be determined in accordance with the modified rules. [436 C] (3) The word 'regulated ' in section 6 (9) of Act 19 of 1952 must be construed in the light of the context in which it is used. [437 D] (4) The word `regulated ' in the section means not hereditary but a hereditary trustee. The word 'control ' in section 2(9) means not hereditary. [438 E] (5) The word management ' in section 3(9) is not defined in the Act. The word management is defined in the sense that on the death of an existing mahant, his chela does not succeed to the office as a matter of course. [439 G] (6) The word administration ' in section 4(9) must be construed as not hereditary. It is not possible to say that there is a succession of As office to another when on the efflux of the period for which a was appointed, there is a vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy. [440 G] (7) The word control ' in section 5(9) cannot be construed as merely a hereditary trustee and not a hereditary trustee because the successor acquires a right only by appointment and the authority to appoint is vested in the assembly of the bairagis and the worshippets. [441 G] (8) The word in section 6 is not defined either in the Act or in the Act, but in the context of the Act. [442 G] (9) The word is not defined by the Act. It is a well established rule of construction that the word 'control' in section 6 of the Act is not defined. [447 G] (10) The word has been used in the sense of 'control ' and not in the sense in which it has been used.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was not justified in convicting the appellant on the sole testimony of PW 4. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was not right in convicting the accused on the sole evidence of PW 4, because the prosecution had not examined PW 4 in the first information report. The High Courts have not considered the intrinsic quality of the evidence of PW4. The High 'Court was not right that the High court in this case had made a correct approach in assessing the quality of the testimony of PW4, and that the High 'Court had not considered the inherent quality of the prosecution evidence. [707E F] 2. The High. Court has not considered the evidence of the sole witness who has stated in the first report that the deceased was only mentioning the name of accused Karunakaran as his assailant, this earlier version appears to be contradicted by the medical evidence. [077E F] 3. The High Curt has not considered whether the evidence of this solitary eye witness has been rejected with reference to the 1 second accused who was on the same boat with the appellant. The High, Court has not examined the evidence of 4th accused in the first instance. The High is not even right that PW 4 stands wholly corroborated by the contents of the FIR. [708F] 4.

The respondent assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax in the hands of the respondent under section 34(1)(b) of the Income tax Act, 1922, on the income received by the respondent. The Income tax Officer found that the respondent was liable to pay out of the estate of the deceased Amarchand and that the income was liable to tax under section 24B (1) (b) of that Act. The respondent 's appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was dismissed. The Appellate Tribunal held that the income received subsequent to the previous year in which Amarchand died was liable to be assessed to income Tax under section 24 B (1) of the Act. The High Court, on reference, held that the amount received by the deceased was not liable to tax as the estate was liable for tax under section 4(1)(a) of the Indian Income tax Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The words "or any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died" in section 24B(1) of that section mean that irrespective of the date of receipt of income receivable by a person, if the income is received before his death or by his heirs and legal representatives after his death, they are liable for payment of the tax just as the deceased would have been liable when the income was received before his life. [707 D E] (ii) The words 'or any tax ' in section 24 B(1) are wide enough to include all income which may be deemed by fiction to have been received by the dead person and which may be assessed to tax under the Act. [708 D] (iii) The words used in section 24A(1) mean that the heirs and legal representative of a deceased person are liable to pay income tax out of his estate. [709 D] (iv) The words in section 24 A(1) refer to the heirs and the legal representatives of a deceased assessee. The words "and legal representatives of the deceased person are not liable to be taxed in the hands o the heirs and Legal representatives who cannot be deemed to be assessees for the purpose of assessment in regard to those years. [710 D] (v) The words of sub section (1) are not wide enough to cover all cases where the deceased person dies before his death and the income received after his death by his heirs or legal representatives after the death of the deceased. [711 D] (vi) The words are wide enough and must be restricted to the cases provided in the three sub sections of section 24B. [712 G] (vii) The words, "or any other tax which would be payable by him if he had died before his death" in section 4(2) of the said Act, are wide enough. [713 G] (viii) The words which are used in sub section (I) of section 24A are wide enough in the sense that the expression "or any taxes which would have to be paid by him under the Act" in section 2(2) is wide enough to take in all cases where a person dies before the death of his heirs and Legal Representatives after his death. [714 G] (ix) The words do not mean that they are not income which may have been deemed by fiction of law to have been earned by the dead persons and therefore they are not liable for tax in the several years of assessment. [715 G] (x) The words must be restricted only to the cases specified in the three subsections of section 24 B and cannot be extended further than the liability for the income received in the previous year. [716 G] (xi) The words should be restricted to cases provided in section 24(B) and not to cases provided for in the two sub sections.

The Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959, were framed by the State Government under section 3 of the Andhra Pradesh Public employment (Requires as to Residence in a part of a State) Act, 1957, which was an Act of Parliament made in pursuance of cl. (1) of article 35(a) of the Constitution. The Act was amended by the Andhra Pradesh Act No. 1 of 1969, which was later amended by the Act No. 2 of 1969, and the Act was again amended by the Amendment Act No. 3 of 1969. The Act provided for the further implementation of the Act. The Act, however, was amended by Act No. 4 of 1969, by which the Act was amended. The Act also provided for the extension of the period of validity of the Act to the extent of the period specified therein. The Act came into force on January 19, 1969. The State Government issued a notification under section 3(1) of the Act, declaring that the Act would apply to the State of Andhra Pradesh. The Act did not provide for any extension of the Act beyond the period of three years. The Act however, was repealed by the Act, and the State Government issued another notification under section 4 of the Act declaring that the provisions of the Act would not apply to the Telengana region. The Act then came into force. The Act received the assent of the President on January 19. 1969, and was published in the Gazette on January 19,. 1969. The appellant challenged the validity of the said Act by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the Act was not applicable to the Telodana region and that the Act did not apply to Telengana regions. The High court held that the impugned Act was not a law relating to the Telangana region and was not applicable in the Telenganas region. The appellant contended that the Act had no retrospective operation and that the impugned legislation was not applicable. The High. Court held that section 3 of Act No. I of 1969 was not applicable and that the appellant was not entitled to the protection of the Act as the Act was a law relating not to residence within the State of Hyderabad. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The Act was not retrospective in operation. The Act had no application to the Telagana region. [122 G] The Act was a temporary Act and was not a temporary Act. The appellant was not a permanent employee of the Telenga region. The definition of "employee" in section 2(1) (d) of the Andhra Act, in so far as it relates to Telenganis region, is wide enough to include a person who has been appointed either directly or by way of direct recruitment or by transfer to any post under the Government of India or any department of the Government of Andhra Pradesh or any department or department of the State Government. [122 D E] The Act did provide for the further implementing of the law made by Parliament. The Act does not provide for the extension or extension of the provisions of a law made by the Parliament. The State Legislature could make any law which prescribes any requirement as to residence within that State or Union territory. [122 E] The State Legislature was competent to make any law in a special case prescribing any requirement as regards residence within that state or Union territory, and the provisions of section 3 of that Act were ultra vires the Constitution. [122 F] The Act, therefore, did not apply.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr post office. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898, and in two of them, he was tried for the offences under section 53 of the Indian Posts Office Act, 1908. The trial court acquitted him but the High Court acquitted him. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The prosecution has failed to prove that these letters were in the exclusive possession of the appellant. The appellant was not shown to have secreted the letter just because it was found in the almirah which was said to have been in his exclusive possession. [413 B] (ii) The fact that the almirah contained a large number of articles belonging to the appellant cannot sustain an inference that he had secreted the articles. [413 C] (iii) The fact of seizure and that the almirah was in the exclusive custody of the appellant was not established. [413 D] (iv) The fact, that the almirah contains a large number, belonging to the father and since he had the key with him it must be taken to be that he was in possession of the almirah and that is why he was not shown as in the almirah. [413 E] (v) The fact whether the almirah contained any large number of items belonging to the deceased or not, cannot sustain an conclusion that he had parted with the articles. The fact that a person is in possession of a large number or a large number is not sufficient to justify the conclusion that he has secreted the article. The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1947. The company was incorporated on April 1, 1948. The balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company were laid before the general body. The balance sheets and profit and Loss account were laid before a general body. On June 30, 1967 the balance sheet and Profit and loss account were laid. The balancesheet and profit & loss account were filed before the general meeting of the company on May 30, 1967. The appellant company was not a director of the company. The balanceheet and profit andloss account were laid up before the general meetings. The appellant was not a Director of the company and its directors could not be heard to say in defence to the charges brought against him that because the general meeting had not been called, the balance sheet, profit and loss accounts could not be laid before it. The appellant contended that the company was not liable under the provisions of section 134 of the 1913 Act or section 220 of the Act as the company was charged with an offence under section 134 of that Act or section 221 of the Act. The High Court held that the appellant was not liable to be heard to the charges under section 134 and that the company could not rely on the balance sheet as an answer to the charge and so, if he was responsible for not calling the general meeting, he could not be considered to be liable under section 134. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : The appellant was liable to be tried under section 134 read with section 220 of 1956 Act. The charge under section 134 is for default in filing copies of the balance sheet or the profit and loss Account before an annual general meeting is made obligatory. But section 134 lays down that after balance sheet and profits and loss account or the income and expenditure account, as the case may be, have been laid before the company at the general meeting three copies thereof shall be filed with the registrar. The failure to do so is made punishable under sub section (4) of section 220 of that Act. [403B C] The appellant was a director of a company and its director could not be said to be liable to be punished under section 134 if he was not responsible for not called the general meeting. [404C] The appellant company could not be held liable under section 135 of the 1913. [405D] The appellant could not be convicted under section 134 because the company was liable to pay the amount of Rs. 1,000/ as costs. [408D] The company could not therefore be held liable for the offence under section 135. [407E] The appellant is liable to be convicted under sections 134 and 220 of the 1913 and section 220 of Act. [414F] The appellant cannot be held liable to be prosecuted under section 134 for the offence of default in filing the copies of the Balance Sheet and profit & Loss account before an annual General meeting is made mandatory. [414H] The appellant had not been a director of any company and its Directors could not be called as Director of the Company. [414D] The offence under section 132 of the 1913 is for default. The appellant could be convicted under the section. [414E] The offence of default is for default and not for complying with the requirements of the sub section (2) of section 134. [414G] The appellant has not been a Director of a company. The company is not liable under section 132. [414A] The appellant, therefore, could not be prosecuted under sections 134 & 220 of the 1956 Act.

The State Government of Hyderabad, by a notification dated January 28, 1950, directed that certain offences or classes of cases should be tried by a Special Court for trial of certain offences or offences or classes thereof. The notification provided that the Special Court shall try such offences or classes or cases or classes of offences or classes as the State Government may, by general or special order, direct. The notification further provided that the provisions of the Act shall apply to all offences or classes and of offences or class of cases. The appellant who was a member of the Special Court, was tried by a special judge for offences under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, and the Special Court held that the offences or classes were not triable by the Special Court and that the Special Judge had no jurisdiction to try them. The appellant contended that the Special judge had no jurisdiction under the Act to try the offences or class or classes of the cases and that the special judge had no power to try them under the Act. Held, that the Special court had no jurisdiction in the matter of trial of offences or offences under section 3(1) Of the Act and the Special judge was not competent to try them in the absence of any special circumstances which may be considered necessary for the trial of the offences or offences. The Special judge had jurisdiction to try the cases or classes or offences or class thereof and the Special Judge could not be said to have jurisdiction to try those offences or classes. The Special Judge had jurisdiction to deal with the cases or class or offences or cases or class of offences or cases. The Special Court had no jurisdiction over the cases or offences or offences and the Special court could not try them. Held, further, that the special court had no power under the Act, to try the accused or classes of persons or cases or offences, or classes of case or classes of Cases, and that the provisions in the Act were not ultra vires the Constitution only because they were not made applicable to the trial of offences. The provisions of the West BENGAL Special Courts Act were not inconsistent with the provisions of article 14 of the Constitution and the special court was competent to try those cases or classes.

The appellant company was a company in which the workmen were employed as casual workers. The workmen were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 95 per month. The petitioner, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1948 49 under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the ground that the income of the family was exempt from income tax under section 5(1) of the Act. The petitioner challenged the validity of the assessment on the ground, inter alia, that the provisions of section 5(2) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 were not applicable to the case of the petitioner. Held, that the petitioner had been given discriminatory treatment even from those whose cases were referred to under section 5 (1) of that Act, and that being so, an enquiry into the validity of that section was really outside the scope of the present case. The petitioner had been denied the benefit of the provisions of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. The provisions of section 34 of the Indian Act, 1922 and section 5(4) of the impugned Act, were not applicable in the present case, because, the petitioner had not been given discriminatory relief from the assessment year 1949 49, and that, therefore, the procedure prescribed by the impugned Act in so far as it affected the petitioner 's case was really outside its scope. The petitioner was given discriminatory treatment only from those whose case was referred to under the provisions of that section and was not referred to the Commission. The petitioner could not be given discriminatory treatment in the present cases because, in the case of persons whose cases were not referred to under s 5(1), the Commission itself found that their cases were not covered by the provisions of s 5(2). The petitioner had not, therefore, been given discriminatory discrimination even from those who were not included in the assessment year 1950 49. The petitioner, therefore, had been given discrimination in the matter of assessment of income tax.

The appellant, a company incorporated in India, was a "commercial establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954. It will bear repetition that the Federation also publishes periodicals, bulletins etc. and issues the same to member free of this Court in R. K. Of course, that profit is ploughed back for the purposes of the Federation as set out in its Memorandum of Association and is not distributed among its members. [352 F] (6) The definition makes it clear that the activity carried on by the respondent was in the nature of a "commercial" and not an association of any individual traders, industrialists or businessmen. [352 H] (7) The definition has to be read in the light of the context in which it is used. [352 A] (8) The definition cannot be read in a narrow or pedantic sense. It is not a mere word of the widest amplitude. It is a word of the same import. It is used in a sense in the sense of a word of a wider import. It may be used in a wider sense than that of a wider sense. [352 D] (9) The definition given in section 2 is wide enough not to include a mere word by which a profits is made. [352F] (10) The definition clearly includes a "Commercial establishment" within it, and no part thereof could be paid as dividend or otherwise, to any member. [352G] (11) The definition also includes a " Commercial establishment" within that meaning. The assessee was a Hindu undivided family consisting of himself and his successors. The income from the family was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer held that the income was agricultural income and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal held that the allowance was revenue income and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income. The High Court, on reference, held that from the language of the letter of July 7, 1837, it was manifest that the right which was conferred was a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. The High court, on reference held that from a true interpretation of the letter dated July 7,1837, it could not be said that the receipt of the assessee was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Income tax Act. The High, Court, on a reference, held in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in holding that from the words of the letter it was manifest, that the right to receive and appropriate to himself the income of the properties or a part thereof in lieu of any beneficial interest in that income was a right which could be said to be the immediate source of the pension. HELD: (i) The source of the income is clearly the arrangement and not land. The source of income is clearly a direct source of the right to a part of the income. [710 B] (ii) The source and character of the income are, therefore, altered when a part of it is appropriated by the appellant as his remuneration, and that is, by the covenant in the deed to receive remuneration for management of the trust. [711 C] (iii) The source is clearly the agreement and not land and the income is therefore, not exempt from tax. [712 D] (iv) The source or character of the assessee is altered when a portion of the income of a trust is appropriated by him as his remuneration. [713 D] (v) The source, of the income, is clearly the direct source of income. [700 D] (vi) The source must be a direct source or direct source of a pension. [714 D] (vii) The source does not necessarily mean a direct source. The source must have a direct nexus with the income. The source is a direct source and not a direct source for the purpose of the income tax. [700 E] (viii) The source in the instant case is clearly the arrangements and not land, and the character of the Income Tax Act is altered when the income is appropriated by appellant as his salary, and that was notwithstanding that computation of remuneration is made as a percentage of the income so received by the appellant. [700 F] (ix) The source was clearly the arrangement, and not land; and the character was not the same as the character in which it was received by the assessee as trustee. [700 G] (x) The source being the arrangement and the source of the Income, it is not agricultural income as defined in the Act.

The appellants, a private operator, were operating tourist vehicles in the State of Karnataka. The appeals were heard by a Division Bench of the High court and the Division Bench held that the decision of a Single Judge of the High Courts was not a decision of a single Judge of the Karnataka High Court and that the decision was not a judgment of a single judge of the High. The Division Bench held the decision of that Court in Sher SINGH 's case that the decision in Sher Singh was not a law decision of the Constitution and that the State Transport Undertaking would have a monopoly. [1016C] 1:5 The decision of another Division Bench in the Sher SINGH ' case was not a case of a single Bench of the same Court. [102D] Sher Singh vs The State of Punjab & Ors., ; , referred to.

The respondent was a dealer in goods. He was assessed to sales tax under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, on the ground that the sale of the goods took place before the transfer of the business under Rule 21 A of the Rules framed under the Act. The respondent challenged the assessment on the ground, inter alia, that Rule 21 A was ultra vires of the power of the State Government under section 19(1) and (2) of the Act. Held, that the rule making power of the Government under section 9 of the Act to create a legal fiction by which the transferee of the business is constituted as the dealer liable to pay the tax in respect of the turnover of the transferor. The rule is not ultra vires of any statute. The rule cannot be utilised to enlarge the scope of section 10 regarding recovery and payment of tax from some other person other than a "dealer" under the Act, and it is not ultra legislative. The rule does not operate on any particular date but as it was published in the Madras Gazette on October 8, 1956, the Act came into operation on that date and not before. The rule was ultra vires. The rule making power conferred on the State Government by section 19(2)(c) of the Madras General sales Tax Act, 1941, was ultra vires the rule making powers of the State. The rule did not operate on the date of the transfer of business under Rule 22 A of the Madras Rules. The rule could not be utilised to extend the scope of the section to the extent of recovery and payment.

The plaintiffs and the defendant were adjoining colliery owners at Kujama. The plaintiffs claimed that the suit land was the property of the plaintiffs and that the suit was not barred by limitation. The trial court held that the defendant had encroached upon the plaintiff 's coal mines on the southern side and removed coal from the encroached portion of the encroached portion. The High Court held that the plaintiffs had failed to prove that the respondents had knowledge of the said encroachment only within three years of the suit. The High court further held that the suit had been filed within three years from 1932 and that the boundary of the suit land had been fixed only with reference to the boundaries given in the lease deed. The High. Court held that there was no evidence on record to establish that the respondents came to know of the removal of coal by the appellant or their possession of the coal removed beyond three years prior to the suit. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the respondents were not entitled to the reliefs prayed for. The High Courts were not justified in interfering with the concurrent finding of fact arrived at by the courts below in respect of the issue of limitation. The High, Court was not justified in reversing the concurrent finding. The High 'Court was not justified to interfere with the concurrent findings of fact arrived on by the courts. The High Curt was not justified on the ground that the findings of fact were based on no evidence. The HighCourt was not right in interfering with findings of fact. The High Tendolkar vs The State of Bombay, ; , followed.

The appellant was a crosscutter. He was charged with misconduct under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders. The enquiry was held and the appellant was placed under suspension pending inquiry. The enquiry officer found that the appellant had committed misconduct and passed an order of dismissal. The appellant challenged the order of dismissal by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the enquiry was vitiated by the misconduct of the appellant and dismissed the petition. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The enquiry was not vitiated by any misconduct. The enquiry is not vitiated by misconduct. The appellant was not given an opportunity to defend the action taken under r. 17(a) and therefore its action could not be upheld as a bona fide exercise of the power conferred. [917 B] (ii) The enquiry is a quasi judicial one and the Tribunal cannot enquire into the causes that led to the termination of service under r. 19(a) or the enquiry under r.18(a). The Tribunal has the right to inquire into the causes which led to the order of termination. [918 C] (iii) The Tribunal has no right to inquire whether the action taken is bona fide or was a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice. The Tribunal has, therefore, the right to enquire into the cause that might have led to termination of service even under a rule like 18(a). [918 E] (iv) The Tribunal was right in holding that the exercise of power was bona fide and was not bona fide. [919 F] (v) The Tribunal had the right to hold inquiry into the causes, that might have been proved, and that the action taken was bona fide. The Tribunal had no right to hold the inquiry. [920 F] (vi) The Tribunal held that the action was bona fide, and was not colourable exercise of the powers under that rule. [921 G] (vii) The Tribunal did not have the power to inquire into any cause that might be shown to have led to the conclusion that the action had been bona fide. It was not open to the Tribunal to go into the causes and decide the question whether the action was mala fide or was not bona fides. [922 G] (viii) The Tribunal could not inquire into the cause which led to termination under r.19(a) if it was satisfied that the action proposed to be taken was bona fides. The Tribunal was not right in holding the exercise of the discretion under r. 20(a) to the effect that the action should be bona fide. If the action was not bona bonafide, it was not bona fouch for an employer to raise a plea of mala fides. [992 B C] (ix) The Tribunal, therefore, had the right of inquiry into the cause, that might be proved to have led the termination of the service under r, 19(a). It could not be said that view is incorrect. [993 C] (x) The Tribunal 's right to inquire is not a mere technicality but a mere technical defect. The Tribunal cannot inquire into the circumstances that led to termination. [994 C] (xi) The Tribunal cannot enquire whether the action proposed by the appellant was bona fide or not. The Tribunal is not bound to enquire into any cause which may have led to terminate the service under the rule. [995 C] (xii) The Tribunal is right in holding, that the exercise was bona fide as the enquiry was not held by the appellant and action was taken under that rule, there was no mala fide. [996 D] (xiii) The Tribunal also held that the appellant failed to satisfy the tribunal when the matter came before it for adjudication that the exercise by the appellant in this case was bona fide exercise.

The respondent was appointed as a pilot Officer in the Indian Air Force and was confirmed in the Indian Army. He was declared unfit by a Medical Board and was confirmed by the Chief Medical Officer. The respondent filed a Review Petition before the High Court contending that he was entitled to be reinstated in service on the pronouncement of the Judgment on 24.3.1988 notwithstanding the fact that his term of office had come to an end on 30th August, 1985 as stated above and no further order of extention had been passed by the Governor. The High Court allowed the Review Petition and made an order reinstating the Respondent in service. The respondent preferred a Review Petition in the High Court. The High court allowed the Review petition and made an interim order directing that the respondent be reinstated in the post in question till 30th August 1985 and not beyond that date unless there was a further extension. The High Curt also directed that the respondent should be paid salary upto the period he was entitled. The High. Court also directed that he should be paid his salary upto the date of his appointment. The respondent challenged the said order of the High Court by filing a Review Petition. The High, Court allowed the review petition and set aside the order of the Single Judge. The respondent 's writ petition was allowed by the High Court and the order of termination was set aside. The High 'Court allowed the Review Application and restored the Judgment of the Single Bench. The respondent then filed a Review petition before the High court contending that he had not urged before the High Curt that the order of appointment issued in his case was not in the nature of a contract and the subsequent orders extending his period of appointment till 30th of August, 1985 were liable to be ignored and that he should have been treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to be appointed irrespective of the merits of the case and the extent of his right. The High .Court allowed the review application and set aside that order. The appellant filed a Review Application before the High. Court contending that the order dated 24.3,1988 was not in any way a contract and that the subsequent orders extended his period of service till 30th Aug. 1985 were liable for be ignored and the Writ Petition was liable to be dismissed. The High ^ Court allowed the Writ Petition and set aside its order dated 24th March, 1988. The appellant 's writ appeal was allowed by this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court had while setting aside the order dated 26.7.1988 passed by the High Cour tial Court on review and restore the Judgment dated 24. 3.1988 passed in the Writ Petition. The interim order did not and could not amount to a direction that the respondent was entitled to continue in service beyond 30th August. 1985 unless there was any further extension. [244B C] 1.2 The High Court was right in holding that the termination order could not be sustained and the Writ petition was liable to fail. [244C] 1.3 The High Court has not given any reasons for setting aside the said order. The High Courts have not given any reason for setting aside that order and the High Court has also not given any reasoning for setting aside this order. [244E] 1.4 The High Court in its judgment dated 24.03.1988 had not given any reasonings for setting aside an order of termination of service passed by the respondent. The HighCourt had not given reasons for setting it aside. The order of termination passed by the appellant was not in accordance with law. [244F] 1.5 The High Court should have given reasons for set aside the said orders.

The appellant, a Judge of the Supreme Court, was appointed as a Judge of a High Court, by the President of India, under the Defence of India Rules, 1962. The appellant was appointed as an Additional Judge of the High Court, and was appointed as the Chief Justice of the High Courts. The appellant challenged the constitutional validity of the said Rules, and the High Court 's order, rejecting his petition, and the constitutional validity thereof. The appellant contended that the Rules were ultra vires the Constitution, and that the Rules, which were framed by the President, were ultra vires, and that, therefore, the Rules were void. The High Court rejected the contentions and dismissed the petition. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The Rules, which are framed by the Parliament under Article 124(4) of the Constitution, are not ultra vires the provisions of the Constitution. The Rules are not ultravi sions of the Constitution and are not ultra virus the Constitution. [216B] 2. The power to punish a subordinate Judge is a power to be found only in article 124(4). The power to impose a punishment of dismissal or removal from office is a power which is conferred on the President by article 124(5) of the constitution. The power of the President to punish a High Court Judge is a clear pointer in the direction that the Parliament has not as yet considered it expedient to enact any such law for the trial of a Judge under Article 124. [216C D] 3. The power conferred on the Governor under article 124(2) is a power of the Parliament under article 124, and the President is the authority competent to appoint and to remove a Judge of any High Court. The power is conferred on him by article 124, but that is not the position in the case of removal of a Judge. The power under article 124 is a clear indication in the direction, that the Parliament had not as yet consider it expedient to provide for the procedure for removal of a judge under Article 124, clauses (4) and (5) of Article 124 read with Article 2 18, and the proviso to Article 124(5). [216C E] 4. The power given to the Governor under Article 124 (4) is a clear indicator of the power that the Parliament is not competent to appoint or to remove a High Court judge. The power has to be found in the Constitution of the Supreme Courts and the High Courts, which have no legal sanction behind it making it justiciable. [216D] 5. The power vested in the President under article 124 (4), is a clear recital in the direction. The framers of the Constitution have clearly visualised that the Parliament did not enact any other law even then for the investigation into allegations of corruption against a superior Judge, instead of the general law was clearly visualised when the alleged misbehaviour is connected with his office. [216E] 6. The word "law" in Article 124(2), has to be given some meaning which would place the burden on the prosecution, howsoever light, to make out a prima facie case for obtaining sanction of the competent authority under Section 6 of the Act and this can be done only if it is read as a part of the scheme under which the public servant is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference to which the disproportion and his inability to satisfactorily account can be inferred.

The appellant was a Sunri by caste. He was a Suniti by caste. The respondent was a Sunti by caste. In the election petition the appellant alleged that the appellant belonged to a smaller caste group within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The Tribunal held that the appellant was a member of the Saha caste and not a member of any Schedule Caste. The High Court, however, held that the respondent was a member and not a person belonging to the Schedule Caste. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant had not been a member of a Scheduled Caste specified in item 40 of the Schedule to the Act and that the appellant did not belong to the Schedule caste specified in item No. 40. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The Tribunal was right in holding that the appellant bore the surname Saha. The Tribunal was therefore right in holding the appellant to be a Sunri. [389C] (2) The Tribunal came to its conclusion that item 40 had excluded from the Sunri caste those who bore the sur name Saha. The appellant was therefore a member of that caste. [389F] (3) The Tribunal had come to its conclusion on the basis of the evidence that the appellant belongs to the Scheduled Caste. The Tribunal came into its conclusion that the appellant fell within the Sunri Caste. The appellant did not produce any evidence to show that there was within the Sunari caste. The Tribunal had also come to its conclusions that item 40 was excluded from the Scheduled Caste specified. [389G] (4) The Tribunal also came to its own conclusion that item No.40 had excluded from Sunri caste the appellant. [389H] (5) The Tribunal took the view that item 40 excluded from Sunari caste those who had not been proved to belong to the Scheduled Castes. The appellant was a contractor. He was paid wages for the period of one year. The appellant paid its employees only as wages for the said period. [445 G] (v) The provisions regarding wages and allowances in the Act do not apply to the case. The Act does not apply to cases where wages are payable in excess of what is prescribed by the Act. [456 G] (vii) The provisions made in the Act by the Act are in the nature of a special provision and in substance constitute a fresh contract between the parties. [457 G] (viii) The provisions under the Act are inapplicable to cases where wage is payable for one day and the wages of the other are paid in accordance with the well recognised principles of fair play and justice to both the parties. The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was prosecuted under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code and was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for two years. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The prosecution which has resulted in the conviction of the appellant was initiated without any sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The prosecution which had resulted in the acquittal of the appellant by the trial Magistrate, was initiated without sanction under section 196(1) Of the Code of Civil Procedure. [1305 D] (ii) The prosecution was initiated without the sanction under section 198(1) and therefore the prosecution was initiated under section 197 (1) of Code of Criminal procedure before the appellant could be prosecuted under section 196 (1) Of Criminal Procedure. [1406 D] (iii) The prosecution, which had resulted into the conviction of appellant, was initiated by the Public Works department without any sanction. The sanction under section197(1) was necessary for prosecuting the appellant under section 409, and the absence of such a sanction was fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. [1407 D] (iv) The prosecution did not bring home the offence of criminal misappropriation or forgery. The prosecution was launched without any sanction, and the conviction was not vitiated by the absence of sanction under section 199(1) or section 197(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code. [1408 D] (v) The prosecution could not be said to have been launched without sanction under the section. The absence of such sanction was fatal. [1409 D] (vi) The prosecution had failed to prove that the appellant had paid the amount to Parma, and the acquittance roll records the payment, and there was in acknowledgment thereof a thumb impression as against his name. If the act complained of was directly concerned with his official duties so that if questioned it could be claimed to have been done by virtue of his office, then sanction would be necessary. [1410 E] (vii) The prosecution case was that the appellant was a public servant and was, at the relevant time, engaged in the performance of official duties. The appellant was, therefore, liable to be prosecuted under s. 409, and no sanction was required for a prosecution under section 197, Criminal Procedure Code, and the prosecution was not barred by section 197(l) of the Act.

The appellant was a resident of Travancore State in the year 1949. He was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the income of the business in the erstwhile State of Travancore. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the information furnished by the appellant, assessed the income of his business in the former State of Travancore, and the loss under the head business in the latter State. The appellant contended that the business losses incurred in the erstwhile state of Travancore were not taxable under the Indian income tax Act, and that the income of business losses incurred by the appellant in the erstwhile territory of Travancore was exempt from tax under the provisions of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer rejected the contention and held that the business loss incurred in the former state of Travancore was taxable under the Income tax Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal, on reference, held that the income from the business in Travancore was taxable as income under the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 and that the loss under section 10 of the Indian Act was not taxable under section 10. The High Court, on reference. held that the profits and loss incurred in Travancore were taxable under the Act and that the profits of the business were taxable under section 12B of the Indian Incometax (Amendment) Act, 1941, and that income from the said business was taxable under section 2(1) of the Indian income Tax Act, and the High Court, in reference, held against the appellant. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the income tax authorities had no jurisdiction to assess the income of a business in Travancore, and that it was not liable to be assessed under the Indian Act. The income tax authorities were not competent to assess the business profits of the appellant in Travancore, because the income tax was not chargeable under the Indian law. The income of the appellant was taxable under Indian Income tax (Amendment) Ordinance, 1941, by which the income tax Act was amended by the Indian Income ' tax (Amendment). The appellant was not liable under the Indian Indian Income tax Acts, but was liable to pay income tax under section 12 B of the Indian Indian Act. Section 12B of that Act was applicable to the case of the appellant, and the income tax officer was competent to assess it. The appellant was liable to be taxed under the Indian Central Act, 1922 as income under Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Acts, 1941, 1941 and 1941, and the appellant was liable under the Act to pay income-tax on the income. The appellant could not be assessed under section 12A of the Indian Central Acts, 1922, as income under that Act was exempt from income tax under that Act. The appellant had not been assessed under the Act, and therefore, the income tax authority was competent to reassess the income.

The appellant company was incorporated in Calcutta. The company was incorporated at Calcutta under which the age of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the age of 55. The company in its discretion permitted an employee to continue beyond that age. The company however, refused to renew the agreement for the age of superannuation at 60. The company filed a petition in the High Court for a declaration that the age of 58 years was fixed at 60 and that the company should be directed to pay the same to the workmen. The High Court held that the company was not justified in fixing the age of 60 at 60. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the company had no power to fix the age of the retirement at 60 and the company was bound to pay the said amount to the workmen who had passed a medical examination. HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the age was fixed at 55. [427 G] (ii) The Tribunal had failed to notice that the trend in Bombay region had been to fix the retirement age at 60. There was no indication at all as to how long ago the age of Retirement in these concerns was fixed at 58 or at 58. The award and agreements on the question of age of retirement about which information is furnished by the various documents on this record clearly show a consistent trend in the Bombay region to fix the superannuation age at 60 and so, the Tribunal considered it to be its duty to enquire whether the conclusion recorded by this Court in some of its earlier decisions as to the relevant trend in the Hyderabad region was correct. [427 C D] (iii) The award and agreement on the question whether the conclusion was correct or not were wholly insufficient to indicate any slowing down of this trend. The Tribunal had not committed any error in holding that there was no slowing down. [427 D] (iv) The award of the Tribunal and the agreement on the questions of age of superannuation about which information was furnished by the several documents on this Court clearly shows a consistent trend. [427 F] (vi) The Tribunal did not notice that the average age of retirement in the Bombay Region was about 60. The Tribunal has also failed to notice this trend. [435 F] (vii) The Tribunal 's finding that the age is fixed at 60 was not correct. [437 G] (viii) The Tribunal considered it not to have recorded any finding on the question as to the age of retire at 60. It also considered the award of the agreement on question of age at 60, and the agreement.

The appellants were tried and convicted for the same offence and received a like sentence. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellants were themselves the dacoits and were not identified. HELD : The appellants were not identified and they could not be suspected to be dacoits. They were merely receivers of stolen property and were not put to any test identification. They were only receivers of stolen properties and were not shown to belong to the traders. They were not identified by law. They were neither identified nor identified. They were also not identified. The circumstances under which the one presumption or the other may be drawn, it is not necessary to state specifically in this case. It all depends upon the circumstances under which discovery of the fruits of crime are made with a particular accused. It has been stated on more than one occasion that if the gap of time is, too large, the presumption that the accused was concerned with the crime itself gets weakened. The presumption is stronger when the discovery of the fruit of crime is made immediately after the crime is committed. [723 D E] The fact that the accused were found in possession of stolen property from some other 20 persons who were the dacoits, does not make any difference. The fact that they were found in the houses of 20 persons and were the dacoits does not make them a class of persons. They were simply receivers of stolen goods from some other source. They were all receivers of stolen articles from some other sources. They were never identified. They could not be identified. They had been identified by law and therefore they could not have disposed of the property to them.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of 'thinner ' within Rule 2(x)(2) of the , filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for a writ of mandamus directing the State Government to include in the list of substances included in the Rules as "Poisons" "the substance commonly known as 'thiner ' containing spirit and other soluble material such as shellac in which the percentage of such soluble materials does not exceed 30%" as poison was left to each State Government to determine what substance they would include as poison. The petitioners contended that since the Act was a Central enactment it was possible of unjust and unjustified discriminatory appli cation as it was left to the respective States to determine what substances they would include, as poison was not included in the Schedule to the Act, the petitioners did not question the finding on any material. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the petition was not maintainable because the petition was filed after the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed under the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Act is intended to regulate the importation, possession and sale of poisons. The Act does not contemplate any power to regulate the possession of any specified poison in any local area in which the use of such poison for the purpose of committing murder or mischief by poisoning cattle appears to it to be of such frequent occurrence as to render restriction on the posses sion of the possession of such poison necessary. [222C D] 2. The Act provides for presumption and states that any substance specified as a poison in a Rule or noti fication issued under the Act shall be deemed to be a poison for the purposes of the Act. The Act has been amended by adding the old Rule by the following Rule: "13 (1) All poisons kept for sale by any licence holder under these rules (except those kept by a chemist, druggist or compounder for the purchase of dispensing or compounding in compliance with the prescription of medical or veterinary practitioner) shall be kept in a box, almirah, room or building (according to quantity maintained) which shall be secured by lock and key in a separate receptacle of glass, metal or earthenware. " The Act is meant to regulate the import, possession and disposal of poisons and the import of such poisons. It is not necessary that the same substance should be declared as poison for the entire country. [222G H] 3. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance as poison on the particular facts and situation prevailing in that area and the need to regu late the possession and sale in that area. [222H] 4. The notification, and its application thereto to any area, would depend on necessity to declare that the substance as poisonous for the purpose for committing murder or injury by poisoning cattle appear to it to he of such frequent occur ment as to render prohibition on the possi sion of such poison desirable. If the Government thought in the circumstances that the posses tion or sale of the same is to be regulated it could not be said that they have no power to regulate. [222A B] 5. The notification is not intended to regulate possession of any particular poison in any particular local area in the State. The notification or its application to a area would depend upon the necessity to declaring the substance as an poison on the specific facts and situation prevalent in that area, and the need for regu lation to regu late the possession and sales in that area.[222C D, 222D] 6.
