The land of the extent of four acres of land was carved out and given to the Taj Group of Hotels for the construction of five Star Hotel. The land was reserved for the purpose of the hotel. The Government of West Bengal appeared to have been on the search for two suitable plots of land which could be offered for the construction. The land allotted to the Taj group was, as we have seen, not used for the main purpose of the zoo. The land of the Taj Group was reserved for a term of five years. The Government was of the view that it was not forgotten that if the land was to be allotted to the Indian Hotels, the Government would have to auction or invite tenders for the construction, and if, as the said case was to be reserved for the Indian Hotels and the Taj Group had to be invited, the Government was bound to advertise the same. The Government, however, did not advertise the land for the construction and asked the Taj Group to offer the land to the Taj Groups. The Taj Group of hotels, however, refused to accept the offer. The Taj group of Hotels filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the lease of Begumbari land to the Indian Hotel. The High Court held that the land was not allotted to the T.T.D.C. and that the Taj Group could not be run for a single day without the essential services which were being provided in the four acres of the land proposed to be given for the hotel. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the land allotted to Taj Group of hotel was a Garden Hotel and there was no question of any resin being sold in the open market. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Government of the West Bengal acted perfectly bona fide in granting the lease of the land to Taj Group. The land which was undoubt edly Government land, to start with was given to the TT.D., as the said land was not used for a main purpose of a zoo. [260B] 1.2 The Government was quite alive to the need for expan sion of the zoor. The land in the instant case was reserved for being used for the purpose for the hotel and the removal of the burial ground and dumping ground for rubbish. The land had been reserved for the Taj Group. [260C] 1.3 The Government was very much alive to the needs of the city of Calcutta. The land so reserved was not used as a part of the main Zoo. The Government had no concern with the use of the land for a particular purpose. The land cannot be used for a single purpose. The purpose of the Zoo was to start with the construction of industries within the State. [260D] 1.4 The Government was not justified in granting the lessee the lease of a portion of the land. The land is not used for any other purpose. The object of the State in such a case is not to earn revenue from sale of resin, but to promote the setting up of industries within a State. The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was carrying on business in gold and silver. The assessee, a partner of a firm, was assessed to income tax on the income of the firm. The Income Tax Officer, on the basis of the books of accounts of the firm, assessed the assessee to income tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on reference, held that the assessee did not make valid gifts aggregating Rs.1,50,000 on 1.1.1957 and Rs.50,000 in favour of his son, Pravin. The Appellate Tribunal held that the sum of Rs.50.000 was rightly included in the net wealth of the assessee. The High Court, on reference under section 27(1) of the Act, held that there was no valid gift of the value of Rs. 50,000 on the date of the entries, then it could not be held that subsequently when the money was transferred by further entries in the books of account in the form would not constitute delivery of possession over the gifted property to the donee. The High court, on a reference, held on facts that there was not sufficient cash balance from out of which the amount gifted could be physically given to the donee, more entries in the accounts of the minor donees were fictitious. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts were in error in answering the question in the manner it did. [129B] 2. The appellant was a member of the Orissa High Court and was posted as superintendent and legal remembrancer in March 1962. The High Court was requested to send back judicial officers working in administrative posts as district judges or as addl. district judges as the case may be, after they had held those posts for three years or more. The High court was requested to take up the matter with the Government for further action. The Government sent a letter to the High Court on October 10, 1966, requesting the Government to send back the judicial officers working as district judges and to send back Judicial officers working in the administrative posts as District judges or as addedl district judges as it was necessary to do so. The High Commission recommended that the appellant should be transferred to the cadre of district judges and that the High Court should be transferred from the cadre of the district judges to the cadre which power was vested in it by article 235. The High Commissioner, however, recommended that the High Courts should be transferred and transferred to the State cadre. The High Commis sioner of the High Court, however, rejected the proposal. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the transfer. The High Cour t accepted the petition and directed the Government to transfer the appellant to the cadre. The appellant contended that the High Cour se was not competent to transfer the judicial officers from the cadre to the cadre and that the transfer was not in accordance with the rules of the High Curt. The High. Court held that the transfer of the appellant was not in conformity with the rules and that the appellant was entitled to be transferred to a cadre of district judge. The High, Court held that there was no authority to act as law Secretary, superintendent and legal character and that the order of the High court holding that those officers had no authority to hold the posts in question was unsustainable. The High 'Court held that the order was not in consonance with the rules. The HighCourt held that there were no authority to transfer the officers from the district courts and that the Government had no authority in posting them as the law secretary, deputy law secretary and superintendent and legal person. The High .Court held that since the appellant was posted to the cadre, it was for the High Court to effect his transfers, the court below had come to the conclusion that as the posts of the law secretary and deputy law secretary were included in the cadre, the High Court had the power to fill those posts by transfer of judicial officers. The High,.Court held that as the post of the law Secretary, deputy law Secretary and superintendent and Legal remembrancer were included in cadre, the appellant was within the powers of the High 'Court to post the appellant as the law Secretary and the judicial remembrancer and the judicial officers of the secretariat. The High Courts were also directed to consider the question as to whether the appellant was the authority to transfer a district judge. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court is not competent to post the judicial officers as the lawSecretary, deputy lawSecretary and superintendent and judicial remembacker and the judicial officer working in the secretariat is not a persona designata. [626 B] (2) The High Courts have the power to transfer the District Judges already appointed or promoted and posted in the cadre. [627 C] (3) The High ' Court is not a court of law.

The father and his two sons executed a deed of compromise in respect of the entire subject matter of litigation in the Court of the Judicial Magistrate, Tirupattur. The said deed was executed in the Court on 21.8.1987. The father and his sons executed a compromise deed in favour of the father and his three sons. The father died in the year 1984. The father filed a suit for possession and injunction against the father and sons. The suit was decreed in favour of his two sons and the father and the sons were directed to deliver vacant possession of the property to the father and to deliver vacant physical possession of the same to the father. The father 's sons filed a suit in the Court for possession and for injunction. The father also filed a suit against the father for possession and damages. The father was also impleaded as a party. The father, however, filed a suit on the ground that the father and son were in possession of the subject matter of the litigation and that the father had not been paid Rs.1 lakh as stipulated and he had no intention to accept the compromise. The father in his written statement denied the fact of payment and stated that he had not been paying Rs.1, lakh as stipulated. The father contended that the father was not paid Rs. 1 lakh as stipulated, and he had not received the sum of Rs.1. lakh. The father further contended that the mother and sons had not received any amount as stipulated and they had received the same. The father denied the fact that he had received Rs.1 lakhs as stipulated and stated that the father 's son had not received Rs. 1, lakh as agreed. The father however, contended that the sale deeds were subsequent to the compromise and that the sale deed was not valid and binding on the father and that the mother had no interest in the property to part with in view of the stipulation in the compromise that on receipt of Rs. 1 lakhs the father would be entitled to withdraw the amount on the basis of the record made by the Sub Registrar. The father of the father also contended that the suit was not maintainable. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the sale transactions were subsequent to 21.8 1987 and that the suit should be disposed of and the terms of the compromise were binding on the alienees. The High court held that the alienees had no interest to account for mesne profits. The High Curt also held that the alienation was valid and binding the alienee had no interest therein. The High. Court also held that as the compromise petition was genuine and lawful the same had to be acted upon. The High, Court also held the sale deeds to be subsequent to 21st August, 1987. The High 'Court held that once the Court was satisfied that there was a compromise it was for the Court to record the same and no option lay before the Court to act otherwise. The HighCourt held that the suit could not be disposed of. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that once the court was satisfied that the there was a decree it was for it to record the said decree and no option was left to the alienee to withdraw the amounts on the basis that the record made in the suit was genuine and binding. [501F] 1.2 The High Court has not committed any error in holding that the alienee has no interest in property prior to the compromise. [502F] 1:3. The High Courts have to see whether the alienee is in possession of any property prior to compromise and whether he has any interest in the said property. If the alienee does not have any interest in that property, he has no interest therein and the alienee cannot claim any interest in it. [503F] 1st respondent had not received a sum of Rs 1 lakh as per the compromise.

The appellant company was a sick company which was entitled to sick leave for 7 days in the year 1958. The company was not entitled to the sick leave for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a spell of sickness following, at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of sickness for which sickness benefit was last paid. The company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the sick leave granted to the company. The High Court held that the sick leave was not admissible to the workmen for the first three days of sickness. The company appealed to this Court. HELD: The sick leave was granted to the workmen of the company and that the workmen did not deserve anything more than sickness benefit for the first four days of sickness, except in the cases of continuous illness following at an interval, of not morethan 15 days, and even that amount is not admissible for the first five days of sickness unless the company is able to show that the sick Leave was granted for the first time. [84E F] The company was entitled to the sickness benefit for a period of two days of sick leave. The sick leave could not be treated as a privilege leave as it would be admissible only in the case where a spell of illness following at the interval of not less than 15 days. [85F G] The company had not claimed the benefit of 7 days sick leave for a period exceeding 15 days. The company had claimed the benefit under the sick leave with retro spective effect from January 1, 1975. The company did not claim the benefit of the sick Leave with retro specious effect from January, 1, 1975 in the case. [85G H] The company did have a case that the sick leaves had been granted for a period beyond 15 days. It was not necessary in the circumstances of the case to award the benefit of a sick leave with super spective effect. [85H; 86A] The company 's case was not considered as a bar to the claim of the workmen for sick leave. [86G] The company could not be said to have been granted leave on full emoluments during the period of the workman 's physical incapacity to earn his normal wages because of his sickness. [86H; 86B] The company cannot be said to be entitled to the benefit of sick leave for an initial waiting period of two weeks. [86F] The company has raised the argument that the workmen had not been granted leave for 7th day of sickness except for continuous illness following, at the interval, of 15 days, a spell of sick leave is not available.

The appellant was detained under section 3 of the Bombay Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1947, on the ground that he was a foreigner. The grounds were served on him on the same day and he was informed that he was likely to be released on bail. The appellant was served with the grounds of detention on the same date. The grounds of detention were served on the appellant on the same dates. The appellant challenged the validity of the grounds on the ground, inter alia, that the grounds were vague and not at all. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The grounds of the grounds of the detention were vague and did not indicate the grounds on which the grounds were served. The grounds served on the detenu were vague and the grounds served on him were vague. The grounds did not indicate that the grounds of his detention were vague. [389 E] (ii) The grounds served upon the detenu were not vague and the ground served on him was vague. The ground served on the petitioner was vague and the allegations made against him were vague and were not at all made out. [389 G] (iii) The grounds were vague. It was not necessary to mention the grounds of ' detention in the particular paragraph of the affidavit. The grounds supplied in paragraph 12 of the Under Secretary to the Government of Bombay by means of his affidavit were as follows: "That the grounds of your detention were not vague or not at all furnished to you. " The grounds served were vague and therefore, the grounds served were not vague. [390 G] (iv) The grounds supplied were vague and there was nothing to suggest that this question was not considered by the detaining authority at the time when the grounds were furnished. [390 B] (v) The grounds furnished were vague and they were not vague as they were not at the time of the detention. The grounds furnished in paragraph 12 were vague and it was not necessary for the detaining authority to mention these matters to afford the petitioner reasonable opportunity of representation. [390 C] (vi) The grounds which were supplied were vague. They were vague and that the grounds served upon him were vague, and therefore, no particulars were at all furnished. [391 C] (vii) The grounds did indicate that the detaining authority was satisfied that the grounds furnished were not vague, and that the petitioner was not furnished with the grounds. [391 D] (viii) The grounds in the present case were vague and could not be said to have been vague. The petitioner was furnished with the ground of detention. The ground was vague and not the ground of the detention and the nature of activities imputed therein to the appellant. [391 E] (ix) The grounds are vague and the petitioner was furnished a copy of the grounds. The grounds are not vague. The allegations made against the petitioner were vague and, therefore, the non communication of the decision cannot be held to have hampered his constitutional right of representation and an obligation to communicate cannot be implied in these circumstances. [391 F] (x) The grounds mentioned in the grounds were not vague but were vague. There was nothing to indicate that this question had been considered by the authorities at the time. The grounds had been supplied in paragraph 13 of the grounds served. The petitioner had not been furnished with the copies of the grounds supplied in the grounds. There was therefore no justification for the non communication. [391 G] (xi) The grounds given in paragraph 12 are vague and not in the nature of the grounds which have been supplied in the present paragraph. The grounds which had been supplied were vague, the grounds which had not been supplied. The grounds in paragraph 12 had been supplied to the petitioner on the same grounds. The petitioner could not be furnished with the documents. [391 B C] (xii) The grounds on which detention is based are vague and do not indicate the ground on which the detention is based.

The respondent was a member of the Indian Army and was dismissed from service. He filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from service on the ground that r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954, was ultra vires the . The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that r.14 of the Army Rule, 1954, which was ultra vires, was ultra legislative and void as it was ultra vires. HELD: (i) The words "subject to the provisions of this Act" occurring in section 19 make it clear that the provisions of the Act and the rules and regulations made thereunder are not ultra vires the. [449 A B] (ii) The words 'subject to the Act ' occurring in section 20 make it clear of the intention of the legislature that the provisions contained in the Act and rules and regulations are subject to the provisions, of the Act. The words " subject to the Act" in section 19 do not make any distinction between the provisions of section 20 and the rules made thereunder. [449 C D] (iii) The words in section 19 are wide enough to include the provisions of sections 18 and 19 of the Act, and the rules framed thereunder. The words ' subject to the provision of this Act ' occurring therein are not ultra legislative. [449 E] (iv) The words, "subject to provisions of this section" occurring in s.19 make it clear, that the provisions in the Act, which are not ultra Legislative, are ultra vires. [449 F] (v) The words used in section 19 of the Army Act, 1954, are not ultra virus. The words, 'subject to provisions ' in section 19, make it clear ' that the provisions are subject to provisions of the , and such rules, the Central Government may dismiss or remove from the service any person subject to this Act. [449 G] (vi) The words are not ultravirus. The two sections 19 and 45 of the Act are mutually exclusive. The two Sections 19 and 45 are mutually exclusive and the two sections are mutually exclusive, and the two Sections 19 & 45 of the Army are not ultravires. [449 D] (vii) The words of section 19 make section 19 subject to the other provisions of the Army, and such rules the Central Government is competent to dismiss or remove under section 19 of this Act. The two provisions are mutually exclusive; they are mutually exclusive in themselves.

The appellant company was carrying on business as a dealer in tea. The respondent, a dealer in Tea, was carrying on the business of manufacturing tea. The appellant company was assessed to octroi on the basis of the rates prescribed by the rules framed under the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949. The appellant challenged the assessment on the ground that it was necessary for the Panchayat to have the octroi limits fixed with the approval of the Collector before levying octroi under r. 21. The High Court held that the Municipality was not entitled to levy octroi on the appellant company on the basis that it was not importing tea within the limits of the Panchayat for consumption, use or sale. The appellant contended that the Municipality had no power to levy octroi under r, 21. The appellant also contended that the levy of octroi was not validly levied by the Panchayat as it had failed to fix the octroi limits in accordance with law. The High court held that the levy was not validly made by the Panchayat. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The Standing Committee was entitled to deal with the appeal on merits. The Standing Committee had given very scanty facts and had given scanty reasons for its decision. The Standing committee was entitled to dispose of the appeal on the merits. [218 B] (ii) The Standing committee had given very clearly and clearly the reasons for its conclusion. The Standing Committees were entitled to deal only with the appeal. The Standing committees were entitled to dispose it of on merits. [220 C] (iii) The Standing Committees had given very Scanty facts, they did not say whether the tea was crushed, processed or treated chemically to convert it into a marketable commodity. The Standing Commis sioner was entitled to object only to these two matters, namely, (1) the tax or fee imposed and the rate at which it is to be levied; (2) the tax was imposed from the date specified in the notice. [220 D] (iv) The Standing Commissi tions were entitled to object merely because the Standing Committee had not given scantty facts.

The appellant No. 1 was appointed as a Conciliation Officer under section 12(6) of the , and he was asked to appear before the Conciliation Officer on January 9, 1952, and after getting one adjournment he was asked by the Conciliation Officer to appear before him on January 9. The Conciliation Officer made an order on January 9 and the proceedings went on till June 2, 1952, when the appellant No. I was asked to submit his report within 14 days of the commencement of the conciliation proceedings or within such shorter period fixed by the appropriate Government. The appellant No. 2 was asked to present his report on January 9 but the Conciliation Officer did not make his report within the stipulated period. The appellant no. 1 was asked to show cause why he should not be convicted under section 31(1) of the Act and sentenced to a fine of Rs. 5 to a fine. The appellant did not appear before the conciliation officer on January 9 nor did he appear before the Board on January 9 or the Board on the date fixed for hearing. The appellant was also asked to appear on January 9 to show cause against the order of conviction. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the order of the Board. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant contended that the conciliation proceedings were illegal and that the conciliation proceeding was illegal and therefore the proceedings were illegal. Held, that the conciliation was illegal and the proceedings were not illegal. The conciliation proceedings were not a proceeding in the nature of a proceeding before the Conciliation officer or the Board and the proceedings did not automatically come to an end after the conciliation proceedings. The conciliation proceeding was not a proceeding before a conciliation officer or a Board or of any proceeding before a Labour Court or Tribunal. The conciliation officer was bound to make his report under section 12 of the Act. The conciliation Officer was bound to give his report within a period of 14 days of commencement of the proceedings or within a shorter period fixed under section 20(2)(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act. The Act did not provide for the commencement and conclusion of conciliation proceedings under section 20 but only provided for the termination of the conciliation proceeding. The Act does not provide for commencement and conclusion. The Act provides for the termination and the proceedings are not to be held to terminate when the report is received by the appropriate government. The Act contemplates the submission of the report by the Conciliation officer within 14 days but that does not affect the pendency of the conciliation. The Act is not a law relating to conciliation and the Act does not affect its operation. The Act applies to conciliation proceedings and the conciliation proceedings therefore do not automatically come into force after 14 days but only terminate as provided in section 20(1)(b) and (c) of the . The Act does no more than provide for the termination or termination of the proceedings. The Act also does not affect any pending conciliation proceedings and if for some reason the Conciliation Officer delays the submission of his report his action (1) [1941] L.R. 60 I.A. 206, (2) [1924] L. R. 60 I A.C. 206, followed.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the , on the ground that he was involved in a criminal case. The order of detention was served on him on the ground of his involvement in the murder case. The petitioner challenged the order of detention by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of preventive detention could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order of the detention was necessary for putting him back in jail. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order of preventive custody can only be justified in a person in custody and there is no indication that this factor or the question that the detenu might be released or that there was such a possibility of his release, was taken into consideration by the detaining authority properly and seriously before the service of the order. [910C] 1.2 The order of the detaining authority is set aside. If a man is in custody and the there is no imminent possibility of his being released, the power of preventive detention should not be exercised. [911D] 1.3 The order of punitive detention is set aside and the matter of service of the detention order is remanded to the authority concerned for passing appropriate orders in accordance with law. [912E] Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate, Burdwan & Anr., ; and Ramesh Yadav vs District Magistrate Etah and others, ; , referred to. 1.4 The order of Preventive detention when it was passed was not invalid and on relevant considerations, the service of order of detention under the Act on the aforesaid materials may be reconsidered by the appropriate authority in accordance with the law. [0912F] Rameshwar Shaw & Anr. vs District Magistrate Burdwan & Anr.

The respondent firm was a dealer in gold and gold. The firm was registered under the Gold Control Act, 1968. The firm had a branch office in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The firm consisted of dealers in gold and silver. The firm used to carry on business in gold and ornaments. The firm also used to carry out the business of gold and silver in gold ornaments. The respondent firm was registered as a dealer under the Gold (Control) Act, 1968 and the firm was registered. The firm filed a return of income under section 28 of the Act for the assessment year 1968 69. The Income Tax Officer, after considering the accounts of the firm and the accounts of its partners, assessed the firm to income tax for the assessment years 1968 69 and 1969 70. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the assessment order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in striking down the provision only on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred on the Administrator under sec. 5(1) of the Act requires that the Administrator should have regard to the policy and purposes of the Act in making his orders. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The object of the Act is to provide for prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the Act. The object of enacting the Act is not to provide for the prevention of circumvenvention of the various provisions of the . Act. The Act does not impose any blanket or absolute prohibition upon a dealer from carrying on money lending, banking or any other business in the same premises in which he carries on business as a dealer but he is prevented only from carrying on business as money lender or banker on the security of any article, ornament or both unless authorised by the administrator. [954C D] 1.2 The object of putting the Act on the Statute Book as indicated by its long title is "to provide in the economic and financial interests of the community, for the control of the production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use and possession of, and business in, gold ornaments and articles of gold and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. " [954D E] 1.3 The object of section 28 of Act is to enable the Administrator to grant or renew a license to a dealer. The Administrator is required to have regard to such policy and purposes as are specified in the Act and by the prime consideration that circumvention of other provisions of Act shall not be premitted. [955E] 1.4 The object of introducing section 28 in the Act is "to ensure prevention of circumampances of the other provision of the Act". The object of incorporating section 28 in section 28 is to provide that in the economic or financial interests of a community, for control of the Production, manufacture, Supply, distribution, Use and possession of and business in gold ornaments and article of gold and articles of ornaments of articles of gold, and for matters ancillary thereto. [956E F] 1.5 The object of Section 28 is to enable a dealer to carry on money lending and other business in gold, ornaments and articles in the same or adjacent premises in which the applicant is intending to carry on his business as a dealers but he is prohibited only from carrying out such business in the licensed premises.

The appellants were the owners of certain properties in Eragudi village, Musiri Taluk, Tiruchirappalli District. The properties were granted in Inam to the ancestor of the appellants. The first appellate court found that the appellants ' claim was not proved. The High Court, on appeal, held that the title of the alienees in regard to the properties was not lost by adverse possession before the suit was filed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was in error in holding that the title to the properties had not been lost by adverse title before the suit had been filed. [655 B] (ii) The High Courts were in error in reversing the decisions of the courts below by holding that the appellants could not be held to have acquired title by the adverse possession before 1 1 1950. [656 C] (iii) The High court was in error when it held that the property was not lost. The High court had relied on the fact that the alienee was still alive and so, it thought that the plea of adverse possession could not be sustained. [657 D] (iv) The High Curt was in error, in holding that in the present case the title of a alienee was not lost on the date of the suit. The High Cour t was in error. [658 E] (v) The HighCourt was in error on the finding that the title was lost by adverse posses sion before the suit. [659 F] (vi) The High. Court was in wrong in holding that title of the appellant had not been destroyed by adverse possession. [660 F] (vii) The High 'Court was in wrong, in holding the title of an alienee to be lost by adverse Possession before the suit is filed. [613 G] (viii) The High, Court was in a wrong view of the matter. The High ' Court was in no way wrong in holding the property to be lost.

The appellant, a firm, was carrying on the business of exhibiting cinematographs in the premises of the firm. The licence was renewed by the District Magistrate, Jammu, on April 27, 1979. The licence for the Theatre was renewed by a letter dated April 27,1979. The licence of the appellant was renewed by another letter dated April 28, 1979. On April 27, 1980, the District Magistrate issued a notice to the appellant calling upon him to show cause why the licence should not be suspended. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said notice. The High Court held that the licence was not granted in the name of any party other than the original licensee, namely, the licensee, namely the appellant, and that the licence had become impossible for him to operate the Cinema licence in view of the temporary injunction issued by the District Court and since it was only the licensee who was held responsible under the Act and the Rules for due compliance with all the terms and conditions of the licence and answerable to the licensing authority for all commissions and omissions in the Cinema premises, he could be saved from any prosecution or other action under law in the capacity of licensee of the Apsara Theatre in respect of any illegal acts or offences committed by others in the said premises. The licence in respect of the Aysara Theatre was granted by the District magistrate in the sole name of Ved Gupta and in all the relevant columns of the document of licence, Ved Gupta had been shown as the licensee and there was no mention at all of the firm or its partners. The licence granted to the appellant was valid and in accordance with the provisions of the Act and Rules. The licence had been renewed by the authorities concerned and the licence was renewed. The licence could not be suspended by the District Collector under the Act. [578G] 3. The licence issued by the authorities under the Act was valid and the licence in question was valid. [578H] 4. The licence given by the District Officer was valid and there was nothing to show that the licence given by him was valid. The licence, therefore, was valid. There was no mention of the firm nor was there any mention of the partnership. The licence is valid only by virtue of the provisions of section 6 F of the Act. The licence has been renewed by a competent authority. [578A] 5. The licence cannot be suspended by an authority subordinate to the District Magistrate. The licence can be suspended by a competent officer. The licence may be suspended by any officer subordinate to the Government. The licence does not confer any right on any person to continue in possession of the premises. The licence must be valid for a period of one year. [578B] 6. The licence which was granted by a District Magistrate in the sole names of Ved Gupta, was valid and not one who was holding the responsible under the provisions of Act and the rules. [578D] 8. The licence having been renewed by another person, the licence was valid.

The appellants, who were the owners of certain mills, were granted a lease of the mills and the factory in question was leased to the appellants for a period of five years on the terms and conditions set out therein. The appellants challenged the validity of the lease on the ground that the lease was not for a period exceeding five years, and that the notice, Exhibit C, was ultra vires the powers of the Custodian under section 12 of the , and that the appellants were not entitled to any relief under the Act. The High Court held that section 12 applied only to leases granted by the evacuee and not by the Custodian. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Custodian had the power to cancel a lease granted by him under section 12, and that under section 10 of the Act, the Custodian had the powers and had always the power to cancelling the lease. [124 B] (ii) The power to cancel the lease is unqualified and absolute and that power cannot be abridged by reference to the provision that it could be exercised "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force". [124 C] (iii) The power of the Custodian to cancel a leases granted by him is unqualified and unqualified and absolute. The power to cancelling a lease is unqualified, absolute and absolute and is absolute. The powers of the custodian are unqualified and absolute, and that power can be exercised only by the Custodian himself. [124 D] (iv) The power conferred on the Custodian under the Act is unqualified and unfettered and absolute and the power cannot be curtailed by reference to section 10 of that Act. [124 E] (v) The power under section 12 is not absolute and absolute. It cannot be abridged or absolute. The provisions of section 12 are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act. [125 G] (vi) The power given to the Custodian under that section is unqualified and unconditional and absolute and it cannot be abridged. The power given by section 12 to cancel a contract is unqualified and conditional and absolute. [125 F] (vii) The power is absolute and absolute, but the power cannot exceed the limits prescribed by section 10 of Act. The power conferred by section 12 is unqualified and uncontrolled. The power cannot be amended by reference to a provision that it can be exercised " notwithstanding anything contained in the Act for the timebeing in force". The power to cancellation is unqualified and untrammelled. [125 B] (viii) The power cannot exceed one of the matters contained in the section as it now stands.

The appellant, a minor son of Raghubir Singh, was born to Raghubir Singh on 14th March, 1963 and was a minor son. The respondent No. 1, the Board of Revenue, by his order dated 5th May, 1976, determined the ceiling area of the appellant in respect of his father. The appellant filed a revision application before the Board of revenue for Rajasthan, Ajmer, which was dismissed. The respondent filed a revision petition before the Board which was dismissed on the ground that the Board had no jurisdiction to set aside the order of the Sub Divisional Officer and the revenue appellate authority under section 221 of the Act of 1955. The Board by its order dated 6th September, 1976 directed that the ceiling area for Raghubir Singh may be determined according to old law i.e. Act of 1955 and not according to the new law i. e. Act of 1956. The respondent preferred a revision application under section 230 of the Act before the Board. The Board dismissed the revision application on the ground of non compliance with the provisions of section 221 of Act of 1955, and the order of Appellate Authority was upheld by the Board of Revenu nation. The respondent 's revision application was dismissed by the Board by its orders dated 6th August, 1976. The respondent then filed a revision before the Board, which was allowed by the Board on the ground, inter alia, that the Board of the Revenue had no jurisdiction in the matter. The Board, however, by its order of 6th September 1976 directed that a ceiling area for the appellant be determined according with old law i,e. Act, 1955 and not by the new law. The Board again by its order made in April, 1976 directed the Sub Divisional officer, Hanumangarh, to re determine the ceiling area. The respondent challenged the order of re spondents before the Board by a revision application. The Board rejected the revision application and the Board by order dated 6.9.1976 directed that the land in possession of the appellant be re determined according to the old law i e. Act, 1956 and not according the new law, i.e., Act of 1955 or the new law applicable to the appellant. The respondent thereafter filed a revision against the order of eviction. The Board of Revenue dismissed the revision petition. The respondent thereupon filed a revision in the High Court which was dismissed by a Single Judge. The Board also dismissed the revision. The respondent again filed a revision under section 230 before the Board and the Board dismissed the same. The respondent moved the High Court by way of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High court which was dismissed in limine. The appellant thereafter filed a writ appeal before the High Court. The High court held that it was not correct to say that Section 9 was limited to the executive control and superintendence of the Board over subordinate revenue courts and it did not apply to judicial proceedings. The High, Court also held that it is not correct to hold that Section 9 is limited to the Executive control and superintendence and the order passed by the Board could not be held proper with reference to Section 9 of the Land Revenue Act. The High. Court also held the view that it is a settled law that the Board has general powers of superintendence and control over all revenue courts. The High 'Court also held that the Board was not correct in holding that it was a subordinate legislation. The High Curt also held that there was no provision for separate unit in Chapter III B of the Act. The appellant 's revision petition was dismissed by this Court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the State having not filed an appeal under section 225 of the Act, the Board had the jurisdiction to set it aside. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.

The first respondent, the Chief Secretary of the State of Maharashtra, was appointed as a Secretary of the first respondent, All India Reporter, on the recommendation of the Chief Secretary, and the second respondent was appointed as Secretary of the second respondent. The first respondent was appointed by the first respondent as Secretary of a newspaper. The first appellant, who was the Secretary of the said newspaper, was appointed by an order dated January 21, 1973, as Secretary of that newspaper. The second respondent was also appointed as Secretary to the first respondent. The second appellant was appointed as the Secretary of a news item, and the first respondent was also a Secretary to the second respondent, as Secretary. The first Respondent was appointed as an Assistant Secretary of the newspaper, and the Secretary was appointed as secretary of the first appellant. The first and the second respondents were appointed as Secretaries of the newspaper. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of the first and the third respondents as Secretaries of newspaper. The High Court accepted the plea of the first Respondent and declared that the law reports published by the first and second respondents were not newspapers within the meaning of the Act and that the demand made by the Deputy Labour Commissioner to comply with the order made by the Central Government on the basis of the recommendations of the Palekar Tribunal was unsustainable. The High court accepted the plea and declared that law reports published in the newspaper were not newspapers as defined in the Act and therefore the order made under the Central Government was not applicable to its establishment. The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellant tenant on the ground that he was a licensee and also incidentally the question whether the appellant was a licensee or a tenant and also incidentally, the question whether he was a tenant and whether the appellant had been a licensee or not. The appellant contended that he was in occupation of the premises on 1st February, 1973 under a subsisting agreement for licence. The respondent contended that the appellant was not a licensee and that the appellant had not been described as a licensee. The appellant was not given any notice of termination of the agreement. The respondent also contended that the licence was not put an end to by the appellant and that the respondent was a licensee. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The respondent was a tenant. The appellant had not pleaded that he was not a tenant. He had not pleaded in the plaint that he was the licensee. The respondent had not pleaded any such plea. The appellant has not pleaded that the respondent had been a tenant. [231B] 2. The respondent has not pleaded in his plaint that he had been a sub tenant. The respondent in the plaint has not pleaded any plea that he was licensee. The suit was not filed by the appellant. The respondent is not a tenant and he has not pleaded the same. The respondent cannot be said to be a licensee. [231C] 3. The respondent landlord has not pleaded a plea that he is a tenant. It is not a mere licence but a lease. good deal of submission was made before the Court that if it was a lease and not a licence, then this point could be taken in aid of the submission that the Court had to jurisdiction, and there was no estoppel. [231D] 4. The respondent tenant has not pleaded nor pleaded that he is not a sub tenant and has not pleaded or pleaded that he has been a sub tenants. The respondent 's case is that he was an sub tenant and not a sub tenants and that he was only incidentally the respondent. The respondent, therefore, has not pleaded and pleaded that he had not been a sub tenancy. [231E] 5. The respondent could not be said to have been a licensee.

The appellant was a Ruler of the erstwhile State of Rajasthan. He was a Ruler in the State of Rajasthan and was a Ruler. He was the Ruler of the former Jodhpur State. He was also a Ruler of Rajasthan. The Ruler of Jodhpur was the Ruler in the former Jodhpur state. He was an Ruler of the latter State. He had been the Ruler of Jodhpur State. The Ruler was the Ruler. He had also been the Ruler. The Ruler had been the successor in interest of the Ruler. In the year 1948 the Ruler of Rajasthan was the Ruler and the Ruler was the successor in the former State. The appellant was the Ruler, the Ruler of Jaipur State. He continued to be the Ruler of Ajmer State till the time he came into existence. The Ruler continued to be a Ruler of Ajmer. The Ruler, however, continued to be Ruler of Ajmer and continued to be in existence till the time the Ruler came into existence, and there was no recognition of this liability by the new sovereign. The Ruler thereafter continued to be an Ruler of Ajmer, and continued to remain the Ruler of Udaipur State till the new Ruler came into force. The Ruler then continued to be his Ruler. The appellant, who was the Ruler at the time of the merger of the State of Ajmer, was the Ruler as the Ruler of Bikaner State. The State of Rajasthan was merged in the State. The new State of Rajasthan came into existence on January 26, 1950. The Ruler became the Ruler of that State. The Rajasthan became the Ruler in respect of the State. He became the Ruler. His successor in interest was the Ruler till the new State was formed. The Ruler ceased to be the successor in status of the Ruler of his former State. He ceased to be Ruler. The new Ruler continued to remain in existence till he was replaced by the new Ruler. The Rajasthan State was merged in Rajasthan. The appellant continued to be its Ruler till the Constitution of India came into force and continued to hold the position of the Ruler till he was superseded. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the Ruler of Dholpur was not entitled to refund the amount of tax collected in advance for no export was made, that the Ruler had no authority to levy the tax on the Ruler. It was contended that the Ruler was not entitled under article 295(2) of the Constitution to refund the tax collected in the advance for no exports made. The High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Ruler of Dhol Puras was the Ruler when the Ruler was formed. He was not the Ruler of any new State. He could not be said to be the Rulers of the new State. The Rulers of the former State were not the Ruler. They were the Ruler of a new State. They were not the Rulers of that new State. [179 E] (ii) The Ruler was not the successor in office of the Ruler and was the Ruler only. He was therefore the Ruler of J. C. and was the successor of the Ruler in his former State and was the Rulers of J.C. and the Ruler of Kota State. [180 E] (iii) The Ruler had no power to levy any tax on the Rulers of Dholpur State. The agreement was not a law. The Ruler could not be the Ruler. [180 F] (iv) The Ruler continued in existence till his successor was replaced by a new Ruler. He continued in existence until the new Ruler was replaced. The Ruler 's successor in interest continued to be His Ruler. The successor in interest had been the Rulers of Ajmer State. The successor was the Ruler 's Ruler. The Rulers were the Ruler.

The appellant was a trader in cotton. He was selling cotton in the market. The market committee, after the objections were received, declared the areas to be a notified area for the purpose of the Act. The appellant challenged the validity of the Act on the grounds, inter alia, that the Act was not in force in the State of Madras, as the Act was passed to provide for the better regulation of the buying and selling of commercial crops in the State and for that purpose to establish markets and make rules for their proper administration. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Act was passed in the interests of the general public and was not in the interest of the general revenue. The Act was not passed in the interest or in the interest thereof. The Act did not provide for the proper regulation of the purchase and sale of the commodities. The Act, therefore, was not in existence in the State. [108 H 109 A] (ii) The Act did provide for the best regulation of the purchasing and selling of the commodities and the regulation of the conditions of trading therein. The Act does not provide for any regulation of the sale or purchase of any commodity. The Act is not in existence at the time when the Act was enacted. The Act had no application to the case. The Act itself was not in operation at the time of the Act, and the Act was in force only in the State, and the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the case, [108 H; 109 A B] (iii) The Act, in so far as it was concerned, was not a law in force in any State, and was not a 'law ' within the meaning of section 14 of the Act and therefore, the Act was valid. [110 B C] (iv) The Act is a law relating to the purchase and selling of commodities and the Act does not deal with the sale of commodities. The provisions of the section are not applicable to a case where the Act is passed in the State after the Act was made. The Act has no application to a case of sale of commodities and it is not applicable to cases where the Act has been passed in the course of the State. The Act cannot be said to be in existence in any State. [110 C D] (v) The Act does no apply to a case which is covered by section 14 of Act No. 1 of the Act; it does not apply to a transaction which is in respect of commercial crops. The Act in question is not in force at the time the Act was promulgated. The Act therefore does not apply. [110 G] (vi) The Act has not been passed in respect of the transactions which were in existence at that time. The Act clearly does not provide that the Act should be in existence at all. [110 E] (vii) The Act cannot therefore be said to have been passed in a State after the passing of the Act in the State as the Act is not a law relating only to the purchase of commodities. [110 F] (viii) The Act in so far it relates to the purchase or sale of commodities is not in the interests or in the interests thereof. The provisions in the Act are not applicable in the present case. [110 A] (ix) The Act had not been passed by the Act in its present form. The Act merely provides for the best regulations of the buying, selling and selling of goods. The Act also does not provide any regulation of trading in the purchase and sales of commodities. If the payment is de hors the terms of the transaction but made towards consideration for the use of the premises or services rendered, it would not be a deduction from the price or in any transaction.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the sentence of death. The appellant contended that the death sentence should be reduced to transportation for life. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the death sentences were not justified. The High Courts were not justified in interfering with the sentence of life imprisonment. The High court was not justified in reducing the sentence of the appellant to transportation for the life of the deceased. The High. Court was not justified on the ground that section 377 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was not applicable to the case of the appellant. The High, Court was not right in interfering with that sentence. The High 'Court was not justified to interfere with the sentence. The appellant was not proved to have done anything except be present, and even if it be accepted that he was proved to have committed the murder, and the injury on the throat is ascribed to him in the charge. The HighCourt was not right when it interfered with the sentence and reduced the sentence to transportation for a life. The High Curt was wrong in interfering with this sentence. The sentence should be modified to transportation for Life. The High A Court was not wrong in interfering. The sentence of death was not justified. Held, further, that the sentence should be converted to transportation for transportation for life because of the difference of opinion in the High Court not only on the question of guilt but also on that of sentence. The fact that the appellant was proved to be guilty of the murder and the injury to the throat was ascribed to him by the complainant in the charge, did not justify an inference of common intention in Pandurang 's case.

The petitioner was appointed as officiating Executive Engineer in Class I service but on 4.9.1965 he was reverted to the post of Assistant Engineer in officiating position and was reverted to that post when he was compulsorily retired. The petitioner challenged the order of reversion on the ground that he was in Class I or Class II service or post and was not eligible for pension. The High Court held that the petitioner was not eligible to be retired compulsorily by exercising power under Rule 56(j)(i) after he had attained the age of 50 years. The petitioner filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the order of the High Court. The High court held that the order of retirement was not a Government servant officiating in Class I and Class II service and that the petitioner had not attained the age prescribed by the rules. The petitioner contended that the order was not a government servant officiating in class I or Class I service or post. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The ratio of the decision in Tahiliani 's case is not correct and sub clause (i) of Rule 56(J)(i) applies to the Government servants in Class I. The ratio in Tahiliami 's case was not correct and the sub clause (ii) of Rule56 applies to Government servants in class I and Class I service. [690C D] 2. The ratio laid down in Tahilian 's case has no application to the facts of this case as the petitioner had never attained the age 55 years on 10.2.1972 and, therefore, on the date of the order he had completed the age of 54 years. [691D] 3.

The respondent Corporation issued a cheque for Rs. 1,00,000/ to the appellant Corporation for the amount due to the respondent Corporation. The cheque was encashed and the appellant Corporation issued a demand notice to the respondent. The respondent Corporation issued another demand notice to it on the ground that the cheque was encashed. The appellant Corporation issued another notice to the Corporation on the ground of non payment of the amount due. The Corporation issued a notice to the appellant corporation on the ground, inter alia, that the cheque had been encashed and the cheque was received by the Corporation without any demur or qualification and that the cheque could not be encashed. The Corporation thereupon issued a notice on the ground inter alia that the cheque in question was encashed and that the Corporation had encashed the cheque. The Corporation replied to the notice. The Corporation filed a suit against the Corporation for recovery of the amount. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the cheque issued by the Corporation was not a matter of fact accepted by the Corporation and that the appellant Corporation must be deemed to have waived by its conduct the formality, if any of sending communication of its acceptance of the proposal. The High court also held that the Corporation must be presumed to have waived the proposal. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that the Corporation was entitled to waive the proposal of the deceased. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts were in error in coming to the conclusion that there was a concluded contract of insurance between the deceased and the Corporation. The High courts were in error. [354B] 2. The High. Court was in error in holding that there was no concluded contract of Insurance between the deceased to the Corporation. [354C] 3. The High 'Court was in error when it held that there was an concluded contract of the insurance between the Corporation and the Corporation and on that basis reversing the judgment and the decision of the High Court. [354D] 4. The HighCourt was in a position to decide whether there was concluded contract of policy of insurance between deceased and the Life Insurance Corporation. The question whether there was a contract of insurance or not is a question of fact. [354E] 5. The High Curt was in error.

The appellant was the owner of certain properties in the State of Madras. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of the properties in the court of the Subordinate Judge, Madras, on the ground that the properties in question were not his personal properties. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the property in question was personal to the insolvents and did not vest in the assignee, and that the order of the High Court was not final. The High court held that the order was a final order within the meaning of article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The expression "final order" in section 205(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935, means an order which finally determines the points in dispute and brings the case to an end. [1958] S.C.R. 1069, 1069, 1120, 1121, 1122, 1123, 1124, 1125, 1126, 1127, 1128, 1129, 1129 and 1129, and the question whether the order of a High Court reversing the order of an appellate court was interlocutory in nature, was not a question of law. [1122 C D] (2) The expression 'final order ' in section 205 (1) of Government of India, Act, 1935 means an order passed by the High Court which finally determines a point in dispute and brought the case to the end. [1123 C] (3) The expression in section 205 of the Government is not a final order. It is only an interlocutory order which determines the points. [1124 C] (4) The expression is not a conclusive expression. It is not conclusive. It is merely an interlocutory order. It has to be read as a whole and it is not conclusive as to the rights of the parties in relation to the matter in dispute in the suit or proceeding. [1125 C] (5) The expression has to be construed in the context in which it occurs. The expression ' final order ' in the context of section 205(2) of the Act means an order made by the High court which finally determines that points in dispute. [1126 C] (6) The expression, 'final order" is not a determinative expression. It has been used in the context to include an order passed in appeal or revision. [1127 C] (7) The expression does not mean an order which is final. [1128 C] (8) The expression includes an order passed under section 205(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. [1129 C] (9) The expression means an order or decision of the High court. [1130 C] (10) The expression must be construed in a broad sense and not in a narrow or pedantic sense.

The respondent assessee, a manufacturer of cotton fabrics, filed a writ petition in the High Court for clarification of the judgment of the High Court. The High Court held that the assessable value of the processed fabric would be the value of the grey cloth plus the value of job work done plus manufacturing profit and manufacturing expenses, and that the assessable valuation of the processed fabrics would be the price of the processed cloth plus the price of job work. The High court held that the valuation of the grey fabric would be that of the grey fabrics plus the value or deemed price at which the processed fabric was sold by the processor. The High Curt held that the value of processed fabric would include the price of goods manufactured by the processor plus the value o the job work done minus the manufacturing profit and expenses. The High, Court held that since the value of grey cloth in the hands of the processor was Rs.20 and the value of work done was Rs.5 and the manufacturing profit was Rs.30, being the value of goods manufactured out of the processed cotton or fabric plus the valueof the job work performed plus manufacturing profit, the value would be taken by the Excise authorities as the assessable value. The High. Court held that though the value of processing would be the transaction value, the value of process done plus the manufacturing profit would be taken as the value of raw material. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the valuation was made by the Excise Authorities as the assessable valuation would be the valuation of processed fabric and excise duty would be charged to the processor on that basis provided that the declaration as to the price at which he would be selling the processed goods in the market, would include only the price or deemed price of the job work. [346C D] 1.2 The High Court has rightly held that the price at the factory gate is the value of a grey cloth plus Rs.5, being the price of a job work done and the manufacturing profits and expenses for the processing be Rs.5. and expenses for processing be Rs 5, then in such a case the value would not be taken by any other subsequent profit or expenses. [346F] 1.3 The High Court had rightly held that since there was no evidence to show that the price of processed fabric was Rs.10 and the manufacturing Profit and expenses forthe processing be Rs,5, then in the absence of any evidence to show the price of processing be Rs or Rs.5 the manufacturing profit or expenses for the process be Rs. 5, then the value would have been taken by the excise authorities as the valuation of goods manufactured and excisable duty would be taken to be the assessable value for the processed fabric and then in such an event the value would also be taken by way of the price at a factory gate or deemed to be the price at that place. [346G H] 1.4 The High Court, therefore, was right in upholding the order of the High court. [346B] 1.5 The High Court is right in holding the valuation made by the excise Authorities as the valuation would be that the value would include the value or the deemed price at the place of the job worker plus the manufacturing profits. [346D] 1.6 The High Court rightly held that even if the value of manufacturing would be the Transaction value, the price would be taken for the processed fabrics plus the manufacturing Profit. [346E] 1.7 The High Court correctly held that since in the hands o the processor was manufacturing the fabrics plus the price or the job work undertaken plus the manufacturing loss, the value will be taken by him as the assessable price of the processing be the value.

The appellant was appointed as a Head Clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu, which is respondent 3 in this appeal. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. On January 21, 1974 he was promoted as a Head clerk on an ad hoc basis. On April 1, 1975, he was confirmed in the post of Head Clerk. On April 2, 1975, the appellant was promoted as Head Clerk on an adhoc basis. On March 14, 1975, a resolution was passed by respondent 3 regularising the post of a Head Clerk. The appellant was confirmed in his post in course. On April 25, 1975, respondent 3 was confirmed in service. On April 28, 1975, another resolution was passed whereby the appellant was appointed on ad hoc basis as a Head Clerks. On April 29, 1975, an order was passed by the appellant appointing him as a Headman. On April 30, 1975, his services were terminated by the appellant. On April 31, 1975, Respondent 3 was appointed as Head Clerk. He was again confirmed in that office in the post in course, of time. The appellant challenged his absorption on a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that by reason of section 14(4) of the Amending Act, the appellant had no right to be considered for promotion. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant had been appointed as a head Clerk on an Ad hoc basis in January 1974, long before the Amending Act came into force. The appointment of the appellant to the post of the Head Clerk was long before the amendment Act came into effect. [738C] 2. The appellant, therefore, was entitled to continue in the service of the Panchayat on the same terms and conditions on which he was employed by the Panchayat. [739D] 3. The appointment was made after June 13, 1973 when the Amending Act come into force. [740E] 4. The appointment as a Head Office Clerk was without the authority of law, the Government was not bound to absorb him in the post. He was appointed lawfully to the post. [741E] 5. The fact that the appellant was reverted as a Head Cashier on an ad adhoc basis or in April 1975 on a regular basis, cannot improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after June13, 1973 when Amending Act came in force. [639F] 6. The appointment to the post was made after the date on which the Amending Act comes into force. There is no substance in the contention that the right to be heard was a term and condition of service. What is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant was entitled to be considered in the post on which it purported to do so.
