The appellant was the Mahant of Math Sauna. He was elected Mahant of Math, Sauna and was elected as Mahant of Math. The appellant filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or the deity and that the Amauli properties were purchased by the Math Saiva. The trial court decreed the suit but included a finding in his judgment that the Amaulik Yati was not a regularly constituted Mahant of Math and that the appellant was in possession thereof as Mahant and was therefore entitled as Sarbarakar to all the properties recorded in the deity Mahadeo Ji or in the name of Mahant Shivshankar Yati. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the fund from which the Amauli property was acquired constituted the personal property of Mahant Shivram and that the income from the property was liable to be taxed. HELD: (i) The fund from which Amauli properties are acquired constituted the Hindu Religious Income Tax Act 1948. The income from the properties of the Math and the deity are the personal property and the income from such properties are liable to be assessed to tax. [666 B] (ii) The fund was not a personal property of the Mahant, the burden of proof resting on the party who makes the claim. [667 C] (iii) The fund is a personal property and not a personal income of the Mahant. The burden of proof rests on the party claiming exemption from the levy. [668 D] (iv) The fund has to be assessed for the purpose of assessing the income of the Math. The income of the institution or the deity is the personal property or the deity. The income is the personal income of a Mahant. The income has to be ascertained in the light of the evidence adduced by the parties. [669 D] (v) The income from property or the temple is the personal properties of the Mahant and the burden of proving that the property can be said to belong to the Math or the deity, is on the party pleading the claim. The burden is on the person who makes the claims. [670 E] (vi) The income of a temple or the deity has to be determined by the person who made the claim. If the person who claims exemption from the tax is the person who is entitled to the exemption, he has to prove that the property cannot be said to be belonging to the Math. [672 F] (vii) The income is not the personal property. The burden to prove that property can be held to belong to a Math or the temple, is on him. [675 G] (viii) The income has been assessed for the year 1950 and the revenue records show that the income of a Math and the temple were transferred by the District Judge to the appellant. The income was therefore assessed for the assessment year 1950 and not for the year 1952. [676 G] (ix) The income was not the personal income. The income had to be assessed in the light Of the evidence adduced. [682 G] (x) The income had been assessed for 1950 and 1952. The income could not be said to have been assessed for 1952. [664 D] (xi) The income could be said to belonged to the temple or the temple. The income, therefore, could not be assessed for 1952 and 1952. [666 G] (xii) The income, however, could not have been assessed in 1952. [667 G] (xiii) The income in the present case had been assessed in 1953 and 1953. The income in question had been assessed at the time of the assessment proceedings. The income thus had to be determined in the light thereof. [667 A] (xiv) The income which was assessed for 1952 was the personal property, and therefore a claim to exemption from the payment of the tax was made.

The appellants were allotted to the respondents ' land in the village of Raikot in 1949. The respondents applied to the Custodian General for allotment of the land in their favour. The Custodian General rejected the application on the ground that the land was not evacuee property. The appellants then applied to the Deputy Custodian General for a declaration that the land in question was evacuee property. On the question whether the appellants were entitled to quasi permanent allotment of the lands in question. Held, that the appellants were not entitled to any quasi permanent allotment. The respondents were not entitled under section 19 of the Act to any quasipermanent allotment of land in the area in question. The respondents could not be said to be evacuee property within the meaning of section 19 of Act. The Custodian was competent to allot any property to a person or to cancel an allotment or terminate a lease, or vary the terms of any such lease or allotment if the allottee or lessee, as the case may be, was a person whether such allotment or lease was granted before or after the commencement of the Act. The respondents had no right to any quasi temporary allotment of land. The respondents did not acquire any right in the property in question. Section 19 of the , provided that the managing officer or managing corporation may cancel any allotment or terminate any allotment or lease made in favour of a person. The respondents ' case was that the property was evacuee property and was acquired under the provisions of the , and the notification issued thereunder was invalid. The respondents, therefore, could not be regarded as evacuee property within section 19 of that Act. The appellants were not therefore entitled to any statutory right in the land in dispute. The respondents having been given a right to quasi permanent allotments, they could not be treated as evacuee property.

The Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission invited applications from eligible candidates for the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women) District Inspectress of Girls Schools/Associate Regional Inspectress of Girls School in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (Women 's Branch) and the advertisement was published on May 5, 1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examination was over, on the basis of the results thereof success ful candidates upto a base limit have to be called to be interviewed. On account of improper feeding into the computation of the total number of candidates, the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the written examination from the interview, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examination. On the other hand, the situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the basis thereof success f or the success of the successful candidates upto a limit of four months. The High Court upheld the action of the Public Service Commission and dismissed the writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in upholding the action of Public Service Commission. [126E] 1.2 The situation could have be appropriately met by set aside the recruitment, and asking for the fresh interview of the two Scheduled Caste candidates on the ground of improper feeding to the computation of total number of vacancies. There was no justification to cancel the written part or the sole objection. [126F] 1.3 The situation could be appropriately met if the Public Service Com mission had decided to cancel the entire recruitment examination and asking for fresh interview of only a group of unsuccessful candidates in the process of recruitment. There was nothing wrong in the procedure adopted by the Public Service commission.

The appellant, who was the original plaintiff, filed a suit for recovery of possession of the Dera and the properties attached to it. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The High Court held that the appellant was not the successor of the deceased defendant and that the suit was not maintainable. The High court held that the appeal had abated and dismissed the suit. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant had no knowledge about the date of the death of the deceased and held that the suit had abated and that there was no ground for setting aside the abatement. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The appellant was not a successor of the original defendant. The suit is for recovery of the D.era and the property attached to it by the appellant purporting to be the de facto mahant of the D, and the appeal could be continued under the provisions of Order 22, rule 10. [488B] 1.2 The suit was filed on the basis that the appellant as the lawfully appointed mahant was entitled to manage the properties of the D and the properties appertaining to it by his election as mahant. The suit, therefore, was not maintainable in view of the fact that the appellant 's predecessor was the elected mahant of Dera. [488C] 1.3 The suit was for possession and management of the Doda and the properties appurtenant thereto. The suit could be continued only by or against the person to or upon whom such interest has come or devolved. The suit may be continued against the person who had filed the suit and thereafter died during the pendency of the suit. [488D] 1.4 The suit was not for possession and the appellant was entitled to be in possession of the properties. [488E] 1.5 The suit was one for possession and possession and the suit was for recovery of a possession. The suit had been filed on the footing that the appellant and his predecessor were the lawful heirs of the deceased. The suit therefore was not maintainable and the suit could not be continued against them. [488F] 1.6 The suit was a representative suit and the suit had to be disposed of on merits. [488H] 1.7 The suit was to be disposed on merits. The suit must be disposed of within a period of three months from the date of its institution. [488A] 1.8 The suit was barred by limitation.

The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board. They were promoted as Assistant Engineers on the basis of the recommendations of the Selection Committee. The petitioners were promoted as Executive Engineers on the ground that they had been promoted as Executive Engineer on the basis that they had acted on the representation made to them in 1979 by increasing the age of retirement from 55 to 58 years. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said amendment of February 17, 1983 by way of a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the amendment of February, 1983 to the Fundamental Rules was not retrospective in operation and that the amendment was not retrospective. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The amendment of February. 1983 to the FR. 22(1) of the Fundamental Rules is not retrospective in nature. The amendment is prospective in nature and cannot be retrospective in operation. [457C] 2. The amendment in the Fundamental Rules to the Fundamental Rule was made by the Government of Andhra Pradesh in exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitution. The amendment was made by a notification dated October 29, 1979 and nothing had happened thereafter. The amendment did not affect the age of superannuation of the petitioners. The petitioners had acted on their representation made to the Government in 1979 by increase the age of 58 years from 55 to58 years in 1976. The Government had acted unreasonably in not giving any previous notice to the employees who had been promoted to the post of Executive Engineer on that date. The petitioners could not be amended retrospectively so as to take away rights which had already accrued to them. [458E F] 3. The amendment made by the State Government in regard to the revision of pay scales was not in accordance with the Fundamental Rules. The petitioners have not been given any previous notice of the proposed amendment to the Fundamental rules. The petitioners cannot be amended retrospectively. [459F] 4. The amendment to the FR 22(1), which was made by Government of Andhra pradesh in exercise of its powers conferred by Article 309 readwith Article 313 of Constitution, was not in consonance with the Fundamental Rule 22(1). The amendment was therefore, bad for a total non application of mind to the relevant facts and circumstances bearing on the question of the age of the retirement of the petitioners, like the petitioners. [460G H] 5. The amendment could not be said to be retrospective in nature and could not be retrospective in effect so as to affect the rights which had accrued to them by virtue of the amendment. [456H] 6. The amendment cannot be said to have been retrospective in operation so as to bring about a change in the conditions of service of the petitioners which had already been determined by the Government. [455H] 7. The amendment having been made by the government of Andhra Pradesh, the petitioners cannot be said that the amendment is retrospective in operation, so as to make it retrospective. [466H] 8. The amendment has been made by a Notification dated September 17, 19,9,1979. The Government of Andhra Praja Parishad was therefore justified in its contention that the amendment to the rule was not retrospective, and that the Government had acted arbitrarily in not giving effect to the said amendment. [406H] 9. The amendment had been made by Government in exercise of powers conferred by proviso to Article 311 read with Article 314 of the Constitution and not retrospective in effect. The amendment, therefore, was not retrospective and could not affect the rights of the petitioners to the posts which had already vested in them.

The respondent filed a return of the goods in the prescribed form and claimed that the goods were not his property. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim. The appellant appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal held that the goods remained the sellers ' property till the goods had crossed the customs frontier and therefore the sales were exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. The Tribunal held that there was no circumstance which would justify a conclusion that the parties came to a special agreement that though the sales were on FOB contracts property in the goods would pass to the buyer at some point of time before shipment. The High Court held that the sales were exempt from tax under articles 286(1) (b) and (c) of the constitution. Held, that the words " a person " in section 10(b) of Bombay Sales Tax Act as a " registered dealer " in section 8(b) mean " a registered dealer to whom he has sold the goods". The words " the person to whom the Certificate has sold the good" in section 8 (b) mean a registered dealer who has given the certificate under section 10(a). The words " any person " in the section are clear and unambiguous. The words ' a person ' in section 10 of the Bombay Sales Tax, Act as a person " instead of the words " the dealer " in the Act are clear and clear. The words are clear and admit of no doubt that the words ' a registered dealer ' in section 8 are clear and there is no reason why the words " any other person " in that section should be interpreted in the same way as the words " an unregistered dealer " in that Act. The words used in section 10 are " a registered dealers to whom he sells the goods". If the words "a person " in s.10(b) are clear and the words "any person " in cl. (b) are clearly clear and admit the conclusion that the goods are not the property of the dealer.

Courts have consistently followed the well settled principle that the High Courts should not interfere with the concurrent findings of fact unless the conclusions are perverse or the conclusions are based on no evidence. [81 F] 3. The High 'Court has consistently followed the principle that the Court has to see whether the findings of fact are perverse or not. The High Curt has consistently followed that the Court should not interfere in a case where the conclusions are not based on no material. [81 G] 4. The High, Court has consistently followed this principle. The High has consistently followed a principle of law that the High 'Court should not interfere unless the conclusions of fact are based on evidence. [82 A] 5. The High is a new statutory right created as a projection of public policy by the Code of 1973, which could not have been in the contemplation of the parties when in 1962, they entered into a contract to adjust their then mutual rights.

The appellant was a dealer in the business of sale of rice and rice. He was allotted a shop in an auction held on 27.3.88. He was given the shop in the black list for future under the orders passed by the Collector. The appellant was given the highest bid. The appellant challenged the order of the Collector by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that there was no requirement specifically of giving any prior notice before black listing any person. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of the collector is under challenge. The appellant is right. But it is an implied principle of natural justice that any order having civil consequence should be passed only after following the principles of natural justice. It is an elementary principle of natural Justice that any order has civil consequence should he passed only after giving the appellant due notice and an opportunity of making representation against the order. [868C D] 2. The order directing black listing of the appellant in respect of future contracts cannot be sustained in law. In that view of the matter, the last portion of the order in so far as it directs black listing of appellant in respect to future contracts cannot he sustained in law, and in the premises that portion of the said order directing that the appellant be placed in the black List in respect of past contracts under the Collector is set aside. [867F G] 3. The order dated 25th March, 1988 of the Collector is under challenge in this appeal. The High court has not expressed any opinion on the correctness or otherwise of the allegations made against the appellant. The appeal is accordingly disposed of.

The appellant LIC, a public limited company, was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of iron and steel products. The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellant LIC on the ground of bona fide requirement of the premises. The appellant contended that the premises were let out to the LIC and that the LIC was entitled to seek fixation of fair rent in respect thereof. The Rent Controller held that the premises was not a vacant site and that the appellant was entitled to claim fixation of fair and standard rent in respect of the premises in question. The Rent Control Tribunal held that the appellant had no right to claim fixation or fixation of fair or standard rent in the premises. On appeal, the High Court held that the Rent Controller had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for fixation of fair Rent in respect of a property which was only a vacant site, and that the claim in the suit for arrears of rent based on the Rent Controller 's order in respect of premises covered by the lease was only a temporary one and that the Rent Control Tribunal had no jurisdiction in the matter. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Rent controller had no jurisdiction under section 4 of the Act to entertain the claim in respect of property which was merely a vacant site. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question whether the appellant is a tenant in or landlord of, the building and the question whether the landlord is a tenant or landlord of the building and that the question whether he is a tenant of or landlord of a building and that he is not a ryot or the land is not ryoti land is a question of fact and exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Rent Controller and, therefore, the question of title to immovable property and that a civil court cannot be barred from examining a claim of title merely because the question may have had to be considered by the Rent Tribunals as a collateral issue in deciding certain applications before them. [570C D] 1.2 The question on which the jurisdiction of civil court is excluded is only the determination as to the fair rent of the premises and not the determination of the rent fixed by the Rent Controller. [570D] 1.3 The question on the question of the exclusion of a civil court 's jurisdiction as well as the provisions of the Act, is only a question of the direct issue before the Rent Controller, and not a question of title. [570E] 1.4 The question on a proper construction of the Rent Control Act, the question on which jurisdiction of the civil court is exclusion is only the determining as to the ' fair rent of ' the premises. If the civil court in this case had come to the conclusion that there is a relationship of landlord and a tenant and that the landlord was entitled to recover the rent from the tenants, it will have to pass a decree in favour of the LIC on the basis of the fair rent fixed by it. [570F G] 1.5 The question on this aspect of the matter is whether the order in the earlier proceedings is to be treated as an order that is null and void or merely one that is valid until set aside, the answer has to turn on the true nature and scope of the jurisdiction conferred on the Rent Control ler under the Act. [570G H] 1.6 The question on what the jurisdiction of a civil Court is excluded is merely the determination as regards the fair rent and then fades out of the picture. In the instant case, on a proper interpretation of the Rent control Act, the questions on which the Jurisdiction of the civil Court is exclusion are only the determination of ' fair rent ' and then fade out of the story. [570H; 570A] 1.7 The question on Which the jurisdiction of Civil Court is excluded, is only the fixation as to the "fair rent of the property".

The petitioner was a respondent who was a respondent in the writ petition. He was a respondent. He was promoted as a Head Constable in the Mysore State. He was given due opportunity to object to the proposed assign ment of a place to him in the seniority list. The petitioner challenged the validity of the seniority list on the ground that he was not heard after the final list was prepared. The High Court held that the petitioner was not heard before the final list of officers on an analogy with the second opportunity which was afforded to a person to be punished after arriving at a decision on the facts of a departmental trial and proposal to inflict a particular punishment upon him, was quite inap propriate. The High court, however, held that the writ petition was premature as the final list had been prepared. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the High Court was in error in holding that the petitioner had been denied relief against the final list. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that a person whose seniority is to be determined under section 115 of the Act must be given an opportunity to object, to the proposed assigned ment of a places to him in a seniority list. [828 E] (2) The High court was right in taking the view that the petitioner 's representation was not considered after the final lists were prepared. [828 G] (3) The petitioner 's petition was premature. The petitioner ' s case was not premature. The High Courts were not justified in interfering with the final list on the basis of the mere fact that the petitioner did not appear before the final lists. [828 D] (4) The petitioner was not entitled to any relief against the provisional list. [829 G] (5) The petitioner had been given due opportunity of putting forward his objections before the final select list was prepared and published as a final list. The only right that could be claimed by the petitioner was to be considered by the final list and published as the final lists had been prepared without due regard to the particular important points which had to be considered before finalisation. [828 C] (6) The petitioner could not be heard to say that he had a right to be heard against the proposed fist. [828 B] (7) The petitioner has been denied the opportunity of making a representation with regard to the two points urged by him. The petitioner has not been able to make out any grounds for interference with the final select lists. [829 C] (8) The petitioner is not entitled to a relief against the finalisation of the final list, which is a matter within the province of the Central Government. [828 F] (9) The petitioner cannot be heard to contend that he should have a further opportunity against even a final seniority list. If he was to have that opportunity the list would not really be final but only provisional or preliminary. [828 A] (10) The petitioner, therefore, was entitled to an opportunity to make a representation with regards to the two point urged by him and to make a proper representation.

The petitioners are partnership firms carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of cut and polished diamonds. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners who were granted Additional licences under the Import and Export Policy 197879 have to be treated at par with Export Houses who have been granted Additional licences on the basis of their exports made during the period 1977 78. The petitioners who are granted Additional licences in pursuance of the Import & Exports Policy 1978 79 have to be treat at par with export Houses who have not been granted Additional Licences under the Import Policy 1978 79 on the basis that not foreign exchange earnings from the exports actually made and the value of such Additional licences is only 10 to 12% of the net foreign exchange earnings. The petitioners, who were granted additional licences under the import and Export Policy 1979 79, have to be considered at par with the Export Houses who are granted additional licences on the strength of their exports. [236B C] 1.2 The petitioners who have been given Additional licences under Import & Export policy 1978 79 have been granted additional licences for the subsequent years and since there has been relaxation in the matter of policy of canalisation of imports under sub para (4) of 246 para 215 in respect of Additional licences granted to Export Houses under the Import& Export Policy 1978 80, the petitioners are also entitled to a similar relaxation. [236C D] 1.3 The petitioners who had been granted Additional licence under the Import, Export Houses Scheme 1978 79 have not been given the facilities which have been given to Export Houses who were granted Addl licences under the Export & Export Policy 1979 80. The petitioners have been granted the Additional licences under import and Export policy 197879. The petitioners were granted Additional Licences in pursuance of this Court 's order dated April 18, 1985 in Rajnikant Brothers, case (supra) and had imported canalised items under the said licence. The petitioners had been granted additional licence under the import & Export Policy 1988 91.

The appellant, a manufacturer of bulk drugs, was manufacturing bulk drugs and selling them to the buyers in packed condition. The appellant, a wholesale dealer, sold the bulk drugs to the buyers. The appellant sold the bulk drug to the buyers, and the packing was not returnable by the buyer. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the levy of excise duty on the value of the bulk drug. The High Court held that at the time of removal the goods were delivered from the factory in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by them, and that the packing was of durable nature and returnable by the buyers to the appellant. The High court held that at that time the goods were deliverable by the buyer to the buyer, and that there was no question of any packing being returnable by the appellant. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the cost of packing could be included in the assessable value only when the packing is of durable character and is returnable by the seller to the assessee, and that since the Act provides for only one exception to this measure, namely, non inclusion of the cost of such packing where the packing is durable in nature and is returnable, by the buyer, to the manufacturer, the value of such packing would have to be included in that assessable value, and that in respect of the goods so sold, the cost of the packing would have been included in the value of goods for the purpose of excise duty. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The cost of packing envisaged in section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act for determining the value of excisable goods is only the "cost of such packing" incurred by the manufacturer and recovered from the buyer except where the packing was in a durable nature. [975C] 1.2 The object and purpose of the levy, the meaning of the expression "assessable value" as interpreted in section before its amendment cou pled with the now well established position that the amend ment intended to make no change in this position, the use of the word "cost" rather than "value" the nature of the other payments referred to in sub clause (ii) all these show beyond doubt that, while generally the normal price for which the goods are sold at the factory gate is to be taken as the assessable value, an addition thereto has to be made where in addition to the price, the manufacturer levies a charge for the packing which is intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placing the manufactured goods on the market. [976C D] 1.3 The object and object of the levy is to provide for excise duty with reference to value of the excisable goods, while generally, the normal price of which the goods is sold at the time when the packing was supplied by the buyer and not the manufacturer. The "cost of packing" referred to in section 4 (4)(d) of the , for determining the "value" in rela tion to any excisable goods is merely the "cost" of such packing which is returnable by a buyer to the manufacturer. [977D E] 1.4 The cost of the drums to the buyer has to be added to the price except where the cost of any packing is of a durable character, and is to be returned to the manufacturer.[978F G] 1.5 The cost of such drums is to be added in the assessable price except where, the packing is not of a durability and returnable to the manufacturer and recover from the buyer, except where the sale is of durability. [978G H] 1.6 The cost of a packing is to be included while computing the assessable value under section 4(1)(d)(ii) of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944.

The appellant was convicted under section 161 I.P.C. and under section 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The prosecution case was that the appellant had demanded a bribe of Rs. 1,000/ for the purpose of running a canteen. The appellant filed a criminal appeal before the High Court. The High Court accepted the prosecution evidence and rejected the plea of the appellant. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the instance of the appellant had not been examined, the solitary evidence of PW 1 is insufficient to hold that the appellant was guilty. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant had a consistent case even from the earliest opportunity that the currency notes found in his possession was the money returned by PW 1, the cir cumstances of the case would probabalise this case of the appellant and the presumption, if any, arising under section 4 is rebutted and the conviction cannot be sustained. [329B] 2. The appellant has not even by preponderance of probability succeeded in rebutting the presumption. The appellant did not even bystand the presumption that the money was returned by PW1, the chal lenging records. The recovery of the currency notes from the appellant was not challenged. The appellant could not, therefore, be said to have been guilty. [331C] 3. The appellant having been convicted and sentenced under section 161, I.P.,C. and section 5 (1)(d), section 5(l)(d) read with Section 5(1) of the Act, the presumption,if any, arising thereunder must further be shown that the explanation is a true one. unless the explanation is supported by proof, the presumption created by the provision cannot be said to be rebutted. [332E] 4. The appellant 's plea that PW 1 had returned the loan and that he had given the money for the Dipawali was probable and there was no conclusive evidence to hold that he was guilty. The appellant, had even by preponderance, succeeded in rebut ing the presumption. The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1947. The company was incorporated on April 1, 1957. The company had its registered office in Bombay. The company, in its place, was incorporated on May 1, 1957, and its registered office was shifted to Bombay. The appellant company was registered on May 1. 1957. The appellant was appointed as an officer of the company on May 1 1957. The respondent company was appointed as the officer of the appellant company on May 2, 1957. On May 1, 1958, the appellant company was appointed an officer of a company. The respondent Company was appointed as a director of the company. The appellant Company was appointed an employee of the company in the year 1957. The Company was appointed on May 1 1, 1957 and the appellant company became the director of the Company on May 1 2, 1957, when the company was incorporated. The company made an application to the Company for a declaration that the company was not a public company within the meaning of section 630 of the Companies Act, 1956. The Company made an application on May 1 3, 1957, for a declaration to the effect that the company had been dissolved. The Company filed its reply on May 1 4, 1957, stating that the company 's name was not included in the register of the company and that the company should be deemed to have been dissolved. On May 2, 1958, a notice was issued to the company to show cause why the company should not be declared as a public company. The company filed its reply. The Company did not file its reply. On May 3, 1958, an application was made by the appellant company for a declaration of its name as a public limited company. The Company also filed its reply to the application. The Company Judge held that the company could not be declared a public company under section 630 of that Act. The Company appealed to the Division Bench. The Division Bench held that the appellant company had no locus standi to file the application for a declaration as it was not a Public company within the definition of section 630. The Division bench held that the application was not maintainable. The Division was of the view that the word 'officer ' in section 630 of H.P. Act, 1956, was referable to existing officer or employee of a company and not to former officers and employees, and that the phrase 'any such property ' used in section 630 was referable to the terms of employment and the right would stand extinguished with the termination to the employment giving rise to an obligation to hand over the property back to the company. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the word "officer" in section 630(1) of H. P. Act, was referable only to existing officers and employees and that the words 'any such properties ' used in the section were referable to existing officers. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'officer" in the section is referable to existing office or employee of the Company. The word "any such property" in section 6(1) is referable to the existing officer and employees of a company, while the word "employee" in section 7(1) refers to the whole of cl. (b) of section 630(l) of H P. Act. [176F G] 2. The word `officer ' in the section means not only the present officer or employee but also the present officer and employee. The word is referable to a new officer or employee. The expression 'any such officer ' in section 6 (1) is relatable to existing officer and employee, and not to past officers or employees. [176G H] 3. The word in section 630 is referable to new officer or employees.

The appellant was therefore entitled to the benefit of the Act as he was a public religious endowment within the meaning section 2(14) of the . [546G] (6) The temple as such was a private and not a private one within the meaning Of section 2(12) of the , [546G H] (7) The temple being a public temple it was a private or public religious endowment and it was not a public religious endowments within the meaning o[557B C] (8) The temple would be a public religious institution within the meaning and the appellant would be entitled to the protection of the Act under section 2(15) of the and the appellant cannot be said to have been a public religious Endowment.

The appellant was arrested and detained in execution of a warrant of arrest issued under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876. The appellant was arrested on the 9th June 1955 and was detained in jail in execution of the warrant of arrest. The appellant challenged the validity of the detention on the ground that section 46(2) of the Bombay Act was violative of article 21 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The provisions of the Bombay District Land Revenue Act are not inconsistent with article 21 of Constitution. The provisions of all the State laws are, therefore, not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act. [157 D] (ii) The provisions in the Bombay City of Land Revenue Act of 1876 are not inconsistent therewith. The provisions in section 46(1) of the Act are not repugnant to article 21 of that Constitution. The State laws prescribe the procedure for the recovery of arrears of land revenue and prescribe the procedure prescribed by the appropriate law of his State for the recovery. [157 E] (iii) The provisions contained in the Bombay Act are not consistent with the provisions contained in section 46 (2) of that Act. The provisions contained therein are not inconsistent. The provisions relating to the recovery of the arrears of land Revenue are not inconsistent and the provisions contained therein cannot be regarded as inconsistent with the other provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. [157 F] (iv) The provisions relating thereto are not inconsistent or inconsistent with the Act. The State law prescribes the procedure for recovery of arrears and clothes the Collector with the power to apply either of the two methods, that is to say, he may issue a warrant of Arrest under section 13(1) and the Collector may proceed to recover from the defaulting assessee the amount specified therein as if it were an arrear of land revenue. [157 G] (v) The provisions regarding the recovery of dues and clothes the collector with the power of apply either of these two methods are inconsistent with the scheme of the Act and the provisions of sections 46(2), 157(1) & 157(2) are not inconsistent, and the provisions in the Act are inconsistent with those provisions. [157 A] (vi) The provisions made in the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1876, are inconsistent with article 14 of the Constitution and are not inconsistent With article 21 of our Constitution. [157 B] (vii) The provisions under the Bombay Act have been made inconsistent with the various provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code and the Bombay City Municipal Act, 1879. The provisions made by the Bombay Act do not affect the provisions of any other law. The provisions are inconsistent with each other. The provisions under section 46(3) of the Indian Income tax Act are inconsistent and the provision in the Bombay Municipal Act, 1888, is inconsistent with the provision of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1879, and the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925, which are inconsistent with section 46(4) of the Code. [157 C] (viii) The provisions are not inconsistent in any way with the provisions in any other law, but are inconsistent with or inconsistent with any other law which is inconsistent with or repugnant to the provisions of a law. [157 H] (ix) The provisions, contained in the Act, are inconsistent and inconsistent with the Bombay Act. The Bombay Act is not inconsistent with any of the provisions of that Act, and the Act is not consistent with any other provisions of that law.

The appellants were the employees of the Bombay Port Trust. The respondents were the trustees of the Port of Bombay. The respondents filed a reference under section 10(2) of the , before the Central Government Industrial Tribunal, Bombay, claiming that the shore crew at the Alexandra Docks should work for 8 hours and that there should be a variable recess of one hour and overtime of three hours should be paid. The Tribunal held that the shores were not fixed for 8 hours but for the period of work. The Tribunal also held that the appellants were entitled to three hours ' overtime for overtime. The Tribunal, however, held that the Shore crew at that time was not entitled to three days ' overtime for the period. The Tribunal further held that the respondents were entitled to the three hours ' wages for overtime. On appeal by special leave, the appellants contended that section 13 fixes the number of hours of work in a normal working day and this number is inclusive of one or more specified intervals. Held, that the Tribunal was right in holding that the shoring of the shore selves in a factory should be so arranged that inclusive of one hour, the number of working days should not spread over more than ten and a half hours in any day. The provisions of section 13 fixes a number of hours for rest and the number of days of work in the week does not exceed 48. The provisions in section 13 fixes one or more hours ' overtime and the number and hours of rest are different. The provisions are not intended to be exhaustive. The provisions relating to the hours of work of an adult worker in a factory are not intended for the purpose of fixing the number of times of work. It is for this reason that a variable recurs is in force at the Prince 's and Victoria Docks and due. The provisions regarding the hours of working in a week are not intended as a matter of course. The provisions for the hours of the work of an employee in a factory shall be so arranged as to ensure that inclusive of the intervals for rest, if any, it shall not spread over less than ten and the number shall be fixed on any day.

The appellant was the tenant of the premises in question. The respondent landlord filed a suit for ejectment of the appellant on the ground of bona fide requirement of the premises. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent landlord for ejectment of his tenant. The respondent filed a written statement and contended that the premises were let out on June 25, 1976 and the accommodation was for the first time assessed for house tax by the Nagar Palika Ghaziabad with effect from October 1, 1976. The appellant tenant denied the allegation that the premises was let out on July 25, 1976. He also denied the allegation of the respondent that the premises had been let out on the date of the suit. The Trial Court decreed the suit for ejectment. The Appellate Court dismissed the appeal. The High Court allowed the appeal and decreed the suit. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 were applicable to the present case and that the suit was not maintainable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of the Act will not apply to the present cases. The provisions contained in sub section (2) of Section 2 of the Act are applicable to the case and therefore the advantage will be available. [167D] 2. The provisions in sub section 2 of Section 2 are applicable to a suit pending on the date when the suit is filed but the suit giving rise to the present appeal is filed on 23rd of March, 1974 long after the commencement of the Act. The suit giving rise of the present appeal was filed on 23th of March,1974 long after the Act came into force. [167E] 3. The provisions under sub section (1) of Section 20 of the Act would not apply to a suit filed on the date on which the suit was filed but the suits giving rise to a present appeal would be governed by the provisions of sub section (3) of Section 19. [167F] 4. The provisions relating to the jurisdiction of the Courts in the matter of granting relief under the Act will be applicable to the suit filed on or before the date of commencement of the Rent Act. [167G] 5. The provisions regarding the jurisdiction of Courts in the matters of granting relief are applicable to suits pending on the dates of commencement of this Act and this is the view taken in Om Prakash Gupta 's case.

The respondent landlord filed a suit against the appellant for ejectment of the appellant on the ground that the appellant had not been able to evict the respondent from the suit premises. The trial court held that the appellant was not liable to ejectment in the absence of any grounds therefor in the notice to quit in accordance with section 3 of the Act as he was a thika tenant within the meaning of the Act. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the respondent was not liable for ejectment in the notice issued by the appellant to quit in respect of the suit premises and that the appellant could not be evicted in the absence thereof. The High court also held that the notice was not a valid notice under section 3 of Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The provisions of the Act were not retrospective and as such could not apply to the case. The provisions of section 4 of the Act would be applicable to the case of the respondent. [775 B] (ii) The provisions in the Act were prospective and as such inapplicable to the case, the landlord had to establish the existence of one of the grounds specified in section 3 in order to succeed. [776 C] (iii) The provisions contained in the Act are prospective and as the result of the provisions of the section, the landlord has to establish the existing grounds in the notice. [778 C] (iv) The provisions relating to notice in section 4 of Act are prospective only. The provisions contained therein are prospective only and not retrospective. [779 C] (v) The provisions regarding notice in section 3 are prospective and the provisions of section 5 of the Act being prospective only, it could not apply. [780 G] (vi) The provisions under section 4 of a. 5 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949 as amended by the Act of 1953, applicable to all suits, appeals and proceedings pending on 21st October before any court or before the controller or before a person deciding an appeal under section 27 of the Act, are prospective only, and as such not applicable to the instant case. [782 G] (vii) The provisions made in section 4 are prospective only if they are retrospective and not retrospective, and the provisions in section 4 being prospective only would apply to the cases of the respondent and not to the appellant. [785 G] (viii) The provisions are prospective only because they are prospective and not retrospective in operation. [786 G] (ix) The provisions which are prospective and which are prospective only apply to the pre Act suits, the landlord having to establish the continuance of one of them, the landlord cannot be said to be a thika tenants within the meaning ofs.3 of the Act of 1949 as amended in 1953. [787 A] (x) The provisions as to notice in s.4 of the Act are retrospective only. [790 G] (xi) The provisions, of section 4, being prospective only and as such applicable to pre Act suits are prospective only in respect of suits, appeals, and proceedings pending before any court, or before the Controller or the person deciding an appel lant under section 27.

The appellant State of Madhya Pradesh was constituted under the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956. The State of Madhya Bharat was constituted under section 2 of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961. The State Government issued a notification under section 127A of the Act, 1973, directing that the tax shall not be levied on lands and buildings owned by or vesting in the Union Government. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification by a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that the State Legislature had no competence to pass the impugned Act by reason of Entry 52, List I read with Entry 24, List II. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The State Legislature had the power to pass a law on the subject and the State Legislature was competent to pass a legislation on the subject. [629G] 2. The power conferred by the State Legislature on the State Legislature to impose the property tax on lands and building is therefore not in conflict with the power conferred by section 69(d) of the Act of 1973. [630A] 3. The property tax is imposed by the State legislature alone. The State legislature has the power to impose the tax. The power to impose property tax is therefore not the same as the power of the State Legislature. [631B] 4. The power of the Legislature to impose property taxes is not in conflict With the power conferred on the Union Government by section 69 of the Act. The power is not in any manner defeated by the legitimate exercise of taxing power under section 69(b) of the , of 1973. The power under section 127 A of the Act is not in the nature of an executive power. The power given to the State Legislature under section 127B of the Act cannot be said to be an executive power of the Government. [632C] 5. The power vested in the State Legislature by section 127A is not in consonance with the power given to it by the State Legislatures under section 69 of Act of 1973, and the State Legislatures have the power to legislate on the subject under the Act of 1956. [633C] 6. The power invested by the State Government under section 127C of the Act to impose property Tax on lands and Buildings is therefore not subject to the provisions of the Act and the State legislature has no competence to impose that tax without following the procedure prescribed by sections 129 and 133 of the Act respectively. [634D] 7. The power which the State Legislature has to pass under section 127D of the Act has to be exercised in accordance with the procedure prescribed under sections 129 and 135 of the Act in accordance with sections 129 and 132 of the Act which are in conflict with section 127C. [635E] 8. The power has to be read in the light of the provisions of sections 129 and 134 of the Act as they stood on the date of the enactment of the Act by the State. [636E] 9. The power exercised by the State under section 127E of the Act 1973 is not in accordance with section 127A(2) of the Madhya Bharat Municipal Corporation Act.

The appellant was a lessee of a land in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The lease was for a period exceeding one year. The lease deed provided that the lessee shall not be entitled to any compensation for the period of the lease. The appellant 's lease was for an indefinite period and the lessee was entitled to compensation for the unexpired period. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the lease was not valid and that the lease should be terminated. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal held that the lease in favour of the appellant had been granted subsequent to July 1, 1945, and that the appellant was entitled to the compensation for the remainder of the period. The High court held that the appellant had not acquired any right in the land and that the Government had no right to terminate the lease. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was not entitled to the protection of the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The third proviso to section 21(1) is that rights created after the notified date but after July 1, 1946, for a period not exceeding one year would also be valid and enforceable by the Government against the person in whose favour such right had been created by reason of section 20(i). [559 E F] (ii) The third proviso is not applicable to the facts of the case. The third Proviso is not applicable in the present case. The appellant was entitled only to compensation for a period of one year. [559 E] (iii) The third Proviso to section 20 (1) is not applicable. The third provisos are not applicable to a case where the lease was for more than one year. It is not applicable where the lease is for a period more than one years. The third and fourth provisos are not attracted. [559 F] (iv) The third and the fourth provisos are applicable only to cases where the lease has been granted for a period beyond one year. If the lease is in the public interest to do so and in such cases, compensation will be payable under section 20(2). [559 G] (v) The third provisos have reference to the rights created after July 1. 1945, for a further period of one years. [559 G H] (vi) The third or fourth proviso is not attracted. The third or the fourth proviso is applicable only to those cases where the lessee has created a right in any land. [559 A] (vii) The third, fourth and fourth provisos have reference only to the rights conferred on the Government by the second proviso. The third, third and fourth proviso are not applicable. [559 C] (viii) The third sub section of section 21(2) is not attracted in the present cases. The third sub sections of section 21 (2) are not applicable in cases where the land is for a term exceeding one year and falling under the second proviso, and the third sub sections are not applicable where there is no express provision to the contrary. [559 D] (ix) The third subsection of section 21 is not applicable because the third sub section has reference to the right created after July I, 1945, for the period exceeding one years. It is only where the conditions mentioned in the third sub sub section are not fulfilled by the Government to avoid the same. If any condition was intended to be super imposed on the right of the Government to terminate the rights created before July 1, 1944, one would have expected those conditions to be mentioned in the second proviso itself. [559 H] (x) The third clause is not applicable when the lease is granted for a term beyond one year, and the lessee is entitled to compensation under section 20 (2).
